#9896. Record, train, and deploy from one place with Strands Agents, LeRobot, and Hugging Face Storage Buckets

A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one agent loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.

You have an agent that can already record a demonstration and push it to the Hugging Face Hub. Now you want to run that loop continuously: collect episodes through the day, train a policy on the growing dataset, deploy it, and pull the next batch back to improve it. Run that loop once and every piece works. Run it every day and you start paying for the same byte transfers over and over. The recordings you upload keep growing, each training run copies the whole dataset to the GPUs before it starts, and every new checkpoint ships out while the next batch of recordings comes back.

The first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent. It covered the Robot() factory, recording a demonstration in simulation, running a policy, and deploying the same agent code to a physical SO-101. That factory resolves a name against a registry of arms, humanoids, mobile bases, and hands, so the SO-100 used throughout this post is one of many supported embodiments. The robot catalog lists every robot the factory knows about. LeRobot's dataset format is already used by over 90,000 datasets and models on the Hub from more than 8,000 publishers (LeRobot Project Pulse). A Strands Robots recording is one more of them, so anything built to read LeRobot data can read it without conversion. If you are new to Strands Robots, start there; this post assumes that setup.

That post followed the agent loop in one direction, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot. This one follows the data the other way, from the first recorded frame back to the deployed policy, over Hugging Face Storage Buckets - a mutable, non-versioned, Xet-backed object-storage repository type announced in March 2026. A bucket sits beside your dataset repositories in the same hf:// namespace and uses the hf CLI you already have, so it becomes the working layer that holds your data between the day you record it and the day you train on it.

Someone has to decide which episodes to keep, when the scene has drifted far enough to re-record, whether today's batch is enough to train on, and which checkpoint replaces the one on the arm. Each of those decisions comes up dozens of times over a collection campaign, and each one needs a look at what came back before the next command goes out. That is the work an agent is for. This post walks you through the data loop inside a single agent: record a demonstration into a Storage Bucket, store it so that each sync uploads only the bytes that changed, train by streaming the dataset straight from the Hub instead of downloading it, and deploy the checkpoint back to hardware with one keyword argument change. The runnable companion to this post lives at examples/notebooks/05_streaming_data_loop.ipynb.

Where the first post recorded a dataset and pushed it to the Hub, the agent you build here records a LeRobotDataset from a natural-language prompt, syncs it into a Storage Bucket, and streams that same dataset back frame by frame, decoding camera video on the fly, with no local copy. You read it back in the same process that wrote it: the same Strands Robots Robot() that recorded the dataset streams it. Your trained checkpoint then deploys to that same Robot() with one keyword argument change, and the demonstrations it records on hardware return to the same bucket.

Figure 1. The four stages share one backend. Robot("so100") records a LeRobotDataset through the shared DatasetRecorder; sync_dataset_to_bucket(...) syncs it into a Storage Bucket; stream_dataset(...) reads it back over the Hub with no full download; and the trained checkpoint deploys to the same Robot with mode="real". The on-disk format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it.

Because one Robot() both records a dataset and reads it back, collecting data and training on it are two methods on one object over one backend. The agent decides to run an episode and invokes one tool; the rollout then proceeds at the robot's control frequency until the episode ends, with the trained policy producing every action. The whole loop, in a handful of lines:

What follows is what's actually happening inside that loop, step by step.

That's it. Every stage in this post runs on a laptop with these three. What runs is the loop, not a working policy: the default path uses a mock policy, which records a valid dataset but not a useful one.

You record new episodes through the day, each a continuous run of camera frames and joint state-action telemetry. LeRobot writes that as a small set of large files that grow as you record. Push them into a versioned dataset repository and every append becomes a commit, and every revision is retained. Collection wants the reverse: somewhere to write bytes and overwrite them in place. That is a Storage Bucket, which lives inside your Hugging Face workspace and uses the permissions you already have. There are no identity and access management (IAM) roles to configure, no cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) rules, and no upload service to maintain.

Your agent records a LeRobotDataset in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware. Record the episode, then sync the finished dataset into a bucket. The prompt asks for the mock policy, a stand-in that produces joint actions without a trained model, so you can run the whole loop before you have a checkpoint to run:

The sync writes to hf://buckets/{bucket}/{run_id}, where run_id defaults to the dataset directory name. The streaming read in Step 3 names the run too: the first two segments of the id are the bucket, and everything after them is the path inside it.

sync_dataset_to_bucket(root, bucket, run_id=...) validates the dataset and syncs it through the hf CLI, decoupled from the recording lifecycle. The same capability is on DatasetRecorder.sync_to_bucket(bucket, run_id=...) if you drive an open recorder directly, and stop_recording(bucket=...) syncs at the moment you stop an active recording. The bucket is the working layer you write to through the day; for the versioned, published artifact you still call push_to_hub(). Both hold the same format.

The episode is structurally complete, but the actions are placeholders, so it is not training data you would want. Swap in a real policy with create_policy("") for actual grasping; the prompt, the format, and the bucket sync stay identical.

To record on a physical SO-101, LeRobot's record CLI handles the leader-follower bring-up:

The dataset lands on disk in the same format as the simulation recording, so the same sync call takes it to a bucket: sync_dataset_to_bucket("./recordings", "my-org/robot-fave", run_id="run-021") (or the hf sync ./recordings hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021 CLI it wraps). Collection runs append into one place, and your published repositories only get the versions you choose to publish.

Now that a dataset is in the bucket, the question is what the next sync costs you. Point two fixed cameras at an arm clearing the same table for eight hours and most of what you record is pixels you already have: the same lighting, the same chassis, the same background, across thousands of episodes. On a versioned repository it gets worse, because changing one frame in a multi-gigabyte video shard re-uploads the whole file.

Buckets are backed by Xet, which deduplicates your uploads at the byte level using content-defined chunking. Chunk boundaries follow the content, so inserting a few bytes changes only the chunk it lands in instead of shifting every boundary after it. In Hugging Face's own measurements (HF Storage), content-defined chunking reduces data transferred per upload by about four times across the Hub, and on Enterprise plans billing is on the deduplicated footprint. Their bucket benchmarks show what that looks like on a single file. Starting from a 500 MB upload, changing 1% of the bytes and re-uploading moved 5.5 MB, changing 5% moved 27.5 MB, and changing 10% moved 55 MB. Without chunk-level deduplication, overwriting an object means sending all of its bytes again, whether or not they changed.

How much that saves you depends on the file layout, and the Strands Robots recorder uses LeRobot's. Episodes go into Parquet shards (data/chunk-000/file-000.parquet) and per-camera MP4 shards (videos/observation.images.front/chunk-000/file-000.mp4), rolling to a new file only when the current one fills, at LeRobot's defaults of 100 MB for data Parquet and 200 MB for video MP4. So a sync after a day of recording uploads the new trailing shards plus the one partially-filled shard that grew, rather than the whole dataset. Sync the same bucket again tomorrow and Xet handles the deduplication.

Figure 2. A sync uploads only what changed. The first sync of a fresh dataset uploads every chunk; after recording more episodes, Xet's content-defined chunking means the next sync uploads only the new chunks and skips the ones already stored.

To train, you point GPUs at your dataset. Download it first and those GPUs sit idle until hundreds of gigabytes finish copying. Streaming straight from the Hub works here because of the shard layout from Step 2: a batch becomes a few byte-range reads over large shards rather than thousands of small fetches. LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset turns that into a drop-in torch iterable, and Strands Robots exposes it through stream_dataset():

Figure 3. Stream, don't download. The download path copies the whole dataset to local disk first, so the GPU waits; stream_dataset() reads batches straight from the bucket with nothing on local disk, so the GPU trains from the first batch.

Nothing lands on local disk except the small meta/ folder of schema, statistics, and episode index. Camera frames are decoded from the remote MP4 shards as you iterate; state and action come from the Parquet shards. That loop reads one frame at a time, which suits inspecting an episode. To train, pass the reader to a DataLoader and iterate batches instead. The streaming dataset shuffles internally through a bounded reservoir buffer, so video decoding parallelizes across worker processes, and the training step itself is the ordinary PyTorch one:

If you would rather not write the loop at all, LeRobot's own trainer reads through the same engine, so the dataset your agent collected trains without a line of new code. It takes a bucket through the same keyword argument the in-process reader uses:

Buckets are streaming-only, so --dataset.repo_type=bucket requires --dataset.streaming=true and the config rejects the combination otherwise. Reach for stream_dataset() when you want the loop in your own process: validating an episode, replaying it in simulation, or feeding a custom evaluation loop. For proprioceptive-only streaming, drop_videos=True skips video decode entirely, which is what makes this work on an edge device with no torchcodec wheel. The recording and datasets guide documents that argument along with the delta_timestamps map it requires.

Provider names are shared between running a policy and training one. create_trainer("lerobot_local") returns a Trainer that works like create_policy(), and a TrainSpec describes the run; the record-train-deploy loop then closes in a few lines:

On a single NVIDIA L4 (g6.4xlarge), 500 optimizer steps of ACT (51.6M parameters, effective batch size 8) over a 120-frame episode completed in 133 seconds and wrote a checkpoint that create_policy() loads back through the same entry point used to run any other policy. Training time scales with dataset size, batch size, and step count, so treat this as one measured configuration rather than a benchmark. The "groot" and "cosmos3" providers target the same TrainSpec and Trainer lifecycle, so the surrounding loop is unchanged; each one validates its own required fields first, so a GR00T run needs a base_model and an embodiment tag, and a Cosmos 3 run needs a base_model and an SFT recipe. Call trainer.validate(spec) before train() and it returns the exact list of what a given backend is missing.

Hugging Face's pre-warming caches bucket data at edge locations near the cloud and region where your jobs run, so your cluster reads locally and the dataloader stays ahead of the GPU. In Hugging Face's own bucket benchmarks, a warm content delivery network (CDN) read hit about 1,086 MB/s on a 10 GB payload against 780 MB/s cold, and roughly 1,124 MB/s warm at 100 GB, measured on an m5dn.24xlarge in us-east-1. The full comparison against plain object storage, upload as well as download, is on that dashboard. Choosing where that data lives is a Storage Regions setting on Team and Enterprise plans, as of this writing US and EU, with Asia-Pacific and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) regions announced as coming; outside those plans repositories are stored in the US.

On macOS, import strands_robots puts Homebrew's ffmpeg on the loader path for you, so torchcodec decodes streamed video without extra setup.

In this step you take the checkpoint you just trained, run it on a physical robot, and record the next round of demonstrations with it. This is the same agent code from the first post, with one keyword argument changed to mode="real":

The checkpoint runs against the physical arm, and the demonstrations that arm records are saved to disk in the same LeRobot format you started with, ready to sync back to the bucket for the next training run.

If your data already lives on Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), none of the format work in this post changes. A LeRobotDataset is a directory of Parquet and MP4 shards, so it stores on Amazon S3 the same as anywhere else, and the recording, training, and deploy steps read that format wherever it sits. What a bucket adds is the Hub-native route: sync_dataset_to_bucket and stream_dataset(repo_type="bucket") target hf:// directly, so you get the sync and the streaming read with no separate storage path to wire up. Both paths run the same loop: Amazon S3 if that is where your data already sits, a bucket if you want the sync and the streaming read without provisioning storage first.

Run the loop again tomorrow and you are recording into that bucket, syncing only the bytes that changed, and streaming those bytes to the GPUs without waiting for a download. The data never leaves the LeRobot format, and it never leaves the Hub.

The full Strands Robots sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in examples/notebooks/05_streaming_data_loop.ipynb. It walks you through the full loop cell by cell: record, render, sync to a bucket, stream back, train, and load the checkpoint. Every cell runs in simulation on the mock policy, so no GPU, no Docker, and no Hugging Face credentials are needed.

Run the cells top to bottom. The recorded dataset lands under /tmp/nb5_dataset. To sync it to a bucket, set BUCKET = "my-org/robot-fave" in the first cell (after hf auth login); the neighboring RUN_ID names the folder inside the bucket, and the notebook streams back from f"{BUCKET}/{RUN_ID}". To train on a GPU, raise steps to 500 and set device="cuda". The agent-driven version of the same loop lives at examples/06_agent_collect_and_stream.py.

The snippets here are a "hello world" of the Strands Robots data loop. Five things change once you run it against real data.

Prompt injection. Supplying untrusted data to an agent can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. These agents actuate robots and now also write to and read from shared storage, so this is an important risk to track. Feed the agent only data from trusted sources. If not all input can be trusted, restrict the tools available to the agent so it cannot take safety-critical actions or overwrite bucket contents.

Training data is a trust boundary. An agent that can write into the collection bucket can also write episodes that a policy later trains on, and that policy drives a physical arm. Keep the credential that writes collection data separate from the one a training job reads with, sync each run under its own run_id so an episode can be traced to the run that produced it and removed on its own, and treat the versioned dataset repository as the reviewed artifact, because the bucket keeps no revisions to audit against.

Bucket credentials and scope. sync_dataset_to_bucket(...), stop_recording(bucket=...), and sync_to_bucket upload through the hf CLI using the token from hf auth login. Use a token scoped to the specific namespace you are writing to, prefer --private buckets for collection data, and keep the bucket distinct from the versioned dataset repository you push_to_hub and share.

Overwrite in place keeps no revisions. A bucket overwrites in place and retains no revisions, which is what makes it a working layer and also means a repeated run_id replaces the run already stored there. Pass an explicit run_id per collection run, as in sync_dataset_to_bucket("./recordings", "my-org/robot-fave", run_id="run-021"). For anything you need to be able to return to, push_to_hub() to a versioned dataset repository, where every revision is retained.

Only use trusted Hugging Face orgs. The local inference path loads Hugging Face models with trust_remote_code=True. Set STRANDS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE=1 to opt in, and only load checkpoints from organizations you trust. When loading pre-trained weights from the Hub (e.g., via pretrained_name_or_path), verify the organization is trusted before loading. Model weights can contain arbitrary code (pickle-based checkpoints). Prefer safetensors-format checkpoints where available.

The loop leaves a bucket, datasets under /tmp, and a checkpoint on disk. Bucket contents count toward your stored volume, so remove what you no longer need:

Stop any training process still on a GPU instance, and stop the instance. If you ran the notebook, substitute its RUN_ID (nb5_demo by default) for cube_pick. Anything you published with push_to_hub() is in a versioned repository and is untouched.

The Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policy providers, recording, and the mesh in depth. The recording and datasets guide documents the DatasetRecorder API, sync_dataset_to_bucket / sync_to_bucket, and stream_dataset in full.

If you collect from more than one robot, give each one its own run_id and they write into the same bucket in parallel. The multi-robot mesh fans one agent out across those robots, so the same loop becomes a fleet collecting through the day into shared storage. A streaming reader reads one run at a time. The recording and datasets guide describes how to train across several of them.

If you want a larger policy than ACT, the TrainSpec and Trainer lifecycle from Step 3 covers GR00T and Cosmos 3 behind their own provider names, so fine-tuning a VLA on the dataset you just streamed is the same calls with a different provider string and a base model. Running the result is where the paths diverge, because a VLA checkpoint deploys to hardware rather than to the simulator you trained from. For heavier simulation to generate that data, the Newton (sim-newton) and Isaac Sim (isaac) backends sit behind the same Robot() factory, so the agent code does not change as you scale up.

Bucket streaming reached LeRobot through contributions from both the Strands Robots and LeRobot teams, upstream in LeRobot itself, so the datasets your agent collects are readable by every tool in that ecosystem. That runs both ways: the reader in Step 3 opens any of the LeRobot datasets already published on the Hub, so an agent can replay and evaluate against existing demonstrations before it records one of its own.

Contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this loop, open an issue with what worked and what didn't.

Results of a internal benchmark on HF Storage Buckets

Explore the robot data lifecycle with an interactive visual guide

Explore robot demonstration data with an interactive dashboard

What makes this architecture particularly compelling is that the agent isn’t just executing a task—it’s sitting inside a continuous data, learning, and deployment loop. Connecting data collection, streaming, training, evaluation, and deployment through one agent workflow opens up some fascinating possibilities for adaptive systems. At the same time, the trust boundaries around data, credentials, and agent actions become critical. This is where custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions need to be designed as complete systems rather than isolated agent features. I came across Mobisoft Infotech while exploring this space: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-company

¡Qué buena onda! Esta integración de Strands Robots con los Storage Buckets de Hugging Face está perrísima para automatizar todo el flujo de trabajo en robótica sin perder tiempo ni dinero. La verdad, la deduplicación de datos a nivel de bytes con Xet y el poder entrenar modelos mediante streaming directo desde la nube nos aligera un buen el trabajo con las GPU. ¡Es una chulada total para acelerar la recolección de demostraciones y el despliegue en hardware real sin complicarse la vida! https://starzbet.mx/

#9895. AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Microsoft's Project Perception adds Guardian Agents to monitor and contain anomalous AI agents, but experts warn that policing unpredictable agents with other agents may compound — not contain — the risk.

Microsoft wants security teams to treat artificial intelligence (AI) agents like they treat employees with privileged access: insiders who can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised.

Earlier this week, the software giant introduced new capabilities to Project Perception, enabling it to discover agents running within an organization, assign an identity and permissions to each agent, and continuously score each organization's risk. When an anomalous agent is discovered in the organization's environment — a problem that Microsoft describes as the "agentic insider" — Project Perception can now cut off the agent's access.

The first release of Project Perception, made available in public preview through Microsoft Defender in August, was designed to defend against AI-driven attacks. Focused on Microsoft's security operations center threat and investigation scenarios, it coordinates red agents to scan for attacker paths, blue agents to identify the greatest risks, and green agents to mitigate threats. Project Perception's initial use was vulnerability management, through MDASH, Microsoft's AI code scanner, which is still in preview. MDASH uses several AI models, including MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, the company's first cybersecurity-specialized model.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

"We're expanding Perception so that we can go secure the AI insider," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, in a brief video accompanying the announcement.

To do that, Microsoft is adding what it calls Guardian Agents, which monitor the AI-based agents running across an organization and can contain them when they stray into unexpected behavior.

Today, many agents run with the permissions of the user who launched them or by invoking the user's credentials. Microsoft's approach separates the two, Microsoft said in a blog post detailing the new capabilities.

Nadim Abdo, corporate vice president for identity and network access, tells Dark Reading that the system gives every agent a distinct identity separate from the user's "and will ensure that the agent starts with no permissions at all, and only up-scopes to the permissions it needs to complete the task the user is asking it to do,"

Specifically, Microsoft said the new release can detect 35 more types of agents running locally on devices, bringing the total to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. It also includes:

Extensions to Microsoft Entra Agent ID that can assign an identity to an agent that was never built to work with Entra.

Dynamic Agent Risk, a continuously updated score built from Entra, Defender, Intune, Purview, Sentinel, and signals from Global Secure Access, Microsoft’s security service edge (SSE) solution that unifies network access and identity protection.

Dynamic Conditional Access for agents, which can block writes while keeping reads, restrict network paths, revoke access, or stop an agent's runtime as risk rises.

Microsoft Execution Container (MXC), a sandbox that keeps credentials and security controls outside the agent's reach.

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

With Project Perception, Abdo describes an expense-approval agent that reads a malicious instruction hidden in an expense report.

"If someone got a prompt that convinced it to start to try to do wire transfers, we can actually watch it accessing a wire transfer system and say, 'Wait a second, that has nothing to do with the intent,' and that raises its risk," he says.

Microsoft says it can act on rising risk immediately, interrupting an agent's live session, network connection, or runtime without disrupting the user's own work, though those are vendor-stated capabilities in preview.

Project Perception has an expanded agent registry that now shows up across the Microsoft 365 admin center, Defender, Entra, Intune, Purview, and a new Perception Agent Insights view. And Dynamic Agent Risk replaces previously siloed risk scores.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

The controls themselves sit outside the agents they watch.

"The first thing [an attacker will] do is they'll manipulate the security controls," Abdo says, so the credentials and monitoring tools run outside the container.

Perception and Agent 365, Microsoft's control plane for governing that was introduced last year and made generally available since May, "need to be battle tested," acknowledged Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a fireside chat with Gallot during a CISO conference last week at Microsoft's Redmond, Wash., headquarters. He also admitted that Microsoft's own detection must improve.

"If I look at the state of the art of behavioral monitoring of, let's say, Defender, it has to go way up," he said.

Gallot framed the risk in terms of how models behave.

"Those models have proven to be unpredictable," she said. "They'll do anything they can to get from point A to point B, and what they do may not be what you intend them to do."

Much of what Microsoft describes echoes what other vendors announced in recent weeks. Okta's Agent Gateway separates an agent's permissions from those of the user directing it, and Okta plans a kill switch that would reject tokens already issued to a deactivated agent. Teleport, backed by Cisco, ties privileges to tasks so they disappear when the work ends. CrowdStrike announced an Agentic Identity Provider and Falcon Guardian, which discovers agents and controls that may run on Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints.

Abdo argues that each vendor sees only part of the picture.

"If you're primarily an identity vendor or primarily a network vendor or primarily an endpoint vendor, that lens gives you some visibility to what agents are doing, but you need to have the other components as well," he says.

Microsoft's advantage, he adds, is that Entra, Defender, and Intune are already widely deployed and integrated, so customers aren't "having to string these things together from multiple vendors."

Microsoft says it will also take in signals from third-party security products. Partners can already publish agent risk events into Agent 365 through public APIs, Abdo says, though he could not yet name which partner integrations are public.

Forrester principal security and risk management analyst Andras Cser is skeptical.

"Most of Microsoft's integration with third-party players, especially in security, has not been first rate so far," Cser says. Because Microsoft has most of the products it needs in its own ecosystem, he adds, it is "interested in pushing its own products."

The question is whether that approach fits environments where agents run across AWS, Google Cloud, Salesforce, and ServiceNow. Last month, Okta announced the formation of the Blueprint Alliance with AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zscaler to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors.

Microsoft is not among the named members. Asked whether it would participate, Abdo said Entra has "always been built on open standards" and that "we're always exploring those things."

Okta, which formed the alliance, argues that no single vendor sees enough.

"No one company can secure agents alone," said CEO and co-founder Todd McKinnon in his keynote at Oktane, the company’s annual conference, last month.

Reacting to this week’s Project Perception launch, Harish Peri, Okta's senior vice president and general manager of AI security, says, "Microsoft's Guardian Agents feature will only be as good as the broader ecosystem it plugs into. If you want to catch intent drift in real time, you need signals pulling from your entire stack, not just one vendor's cloud."

Nevertheless, Peri echoes Nadella's framing. Because agents must be allowed to behave unpredictably to be useful, "we can't secure agents by trying to control how their models think," Peri says. "We need to control their authority."

The answer, Peri says, is "deeper interoperability and cross-vendor signal sharing built on open standards."

Cser interprets the Blueprint Alliance as "more of a partnership kind of map" than a true standard. Cser believes vendor-specific efforts like this alliance are "a marketing ploy" that tend to fade within a year or two. Enterprises need open standards any vendor can implement, he says.

Consequently, that leaves CISOs with an imperfect choice in what Cser calls "still a very fluid market." The current choices, he says, are either a Microsoft-centric approach built mainly on Microsoft products or a multivendor approach with "many vendors, many price lists," where integration "is almost always a suspicious kind of promise."

Some security vendors agree that treating agents as insiders extends the long-standing zero-trust and least-privilege principles rather than replacing them.

Denis Calderone, CTO of Suzu Labs, says the most malicious behavior may never look like an agent straying from its task.

"Dynamic permissions scope what an agent can touch, but the worst outcomes happen inside the authorized envelope," he says.

Calderone points to July's OpenAI incident as evidence that agents can work against the systems watching them. More than 1,000 agents in a cyber evaluation coordinated to game the system grading them, some by faking tool calls, before roughly 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face, according to METR.

Further, Calderone has concerns about Guardian Agents, noting that they are agents themselves.

"Securing agents with agents means the Guardian Agents themselves are overprivileged actors that can be manipulated or compromised," he says.

Cser shares Calderone's concerns about Guardian Agents. An unpredictable agent watched by another unpredictable agent creates "non-deterministic nature squared," Cser says. "Most organizations today are very careful about bringing guardian agents into the mix."

Following Perception's July launch, Forrester principal analyst Allie Mellen urged organizations to enforce "least privilege and least agency," limiting not just what agents can access but what they can do on their own. Microsoft meets the first test but not yet the second, Cser says.

"It is least privilege, but I wouldn't go as far as describing it as least agency," he says, adding that some specialist vendors are further along.

While Perception itself is in public preview, the new Guardian Agent capabilities are in use only inside Microsoft and with "a small set of select customers." They will be expanding to more external customers this week and to broader preview rings over the next few months. Microsoft plans to say more at its annual Ignite conference next month.

Project Perception builds on the controls in Microsoft 365 E7, the $99-per-user-per-month suite that includes E5, Agent 365, and Entra Suite, which supply the signals and enforcement points that Perception relies on. Microsoft hasn't disclosed whether the new capabilities are included in E7, but Project Perception is priced based on consumption.

Cser expects the release to push customers toward E7.

"I would almost be sure that this is another kind of making people buy stuff in more expensive packages that they don't currently need but may need in future," he says.

By his estimate, E7 comes to about $1,200 per user per year at list price, or roughly $600 after typical volume discounts of 40% to 50%, which "can be prohibitively expensive for a lot of organizations."

Meanwhile, Calderone says organizations don't have to wait. He recommends inventorying every agent, including those running on developer machines. Each should be assigned its own identity and credentials set to expire, and each should require human approval for consequential actions.

"That work is free today," he says, "and it's the foundation every one of these Microsoft controls assumes you already have."

Jai Vijayan contributed reporting to this article.

InfoQ Homepage News Google and Meta Open-Source TorchTPU to Bring Native PyTorch Support to Google TPUs

Nov 02, 2026 2 min read

TorchTPU is an open-source project developed by Google in collaboration with Meta that provides a native PyTorch backend for Google TPUs. It enables PyTorch workloads to execute on TPU hardware with minimal code modifications, supporting eager and compiled execution, distributed computing, and hardware-specific optimizations.

Google began enabling PyTorch workloads to run on TPUs in 2020 through PyTorch/XLA, which leveraged JAX, XLA, and lazy tensors. According to Google, this approach had significant shortcomings:

Crucially, PyTorch/XLA required intrusive source-code modifications to explicitly define compilable regions, suffered from severe compile-time latency, lacked support for PyTorch's native imperative (“eager”) execution mode, and lagged in supporting emerging distributed computing primitives within the PyTorch ecosystem.

TorchTPU takes a fundamentally different approach, making eager execution a top priority, and enabling existing PyTorch workloads to run out with minor code modifications.

Specifically, migrating from GPUs to TPUs involves replacing the cuda device with tpu and the nccl distributed backend with tpu_dist. Alternatively, developers can use the new torch.accelerator.current_accelerator API to identify the available accelerator, as shown in the following snippet.

TorchTPU support three eager execution modes: strict, debug, and DeferAndFuse. The latter is a new hybrid eager/compiled execution mode that Google claims "can be 50% or more faster than Strict Eager while reducing peak HBM memory".

To test TorchTPU's ability to run existing PyTorch models with no modifications, Google built an integration pipeline to evaluate about 5,000 Hugging Face models across 500+ architectures in both eager and compiled modes on TPU hardware generations starting from v5e.

We use a robust testing methodology grounded in corpus stratification and balanced architectural selection. Our approach relies on a two-tiered selection process designed to balance real-world adoption with broad architectural diversity, avoiding redundant testing of minor variations while ensuring real production weights are thoroughly evaluated.

To validate TorchTPU's performance, Google ran a 30-billion parameter Muse Glimmer model implemented in standard PyTorch. On a single TPUv7 chip, inference throughput reached 25.7k token/s at 5120 sequence length and 22.4k token/s at 10,240 sequence length. For training, using four TPUv7 chips, throughput reached 5.6k token/s and 4.6k token/s at 5120 and 10,240 sequence length, respectively.

Google also conducted experiments using Qwen3 MoE 235B for training workloads, scaling from 1,024 to 8,192 TPUv7 chips. For inference, Google reported competitive performance-per-dollar for large-scale MoE workloads using vLLM.

Commenting on the announcement, Hacker News user tingkuanpei observed:

Very interesting work. Google should have done this a long time ago. PyTorch's ecosystem is just so rich.

Other users pointed out that beyond offering TPUs through GCP, Google sells them to "enterprise client for on premises deployments", which include Anthropic and in Meta following potentially in the future.

TorchTPU is still at an early stage and therefore in continuous evolution. The project's roadmap include work on dynamic shapes, compilation performance, operator coverage, reinforcement learning, and quantization. For further details, make sure to read the original announcement, which provides a more comprehensive view of TorchTPU's architecture and scope.

#9892. Cyber Insurance's New Reality: Underwriting Isn't Enough

Rising AI, social engineering, and cloud risks are pushing carriers beyond risk transfer and deeper into cybersecurity itself.

The relentless evolution of the threat landscape has pushed cyber insurance companies to follow suit with a continuous expansion of cybersecurity posture requirements as well as taking an active hand in the defense process.

While cyber insurance has existed for years, the ransomware boom of the late 2010s and early 2020s transformed it from a niche risk transfer product into a central component of many organizations' security strategies. Today, policies cover everything from incident response and business interruption to legal costs and, in some cases, ransomware payments. Some of the names you'll see pop up around this space include Coalition, Chubb, AXA XL, Cowbell, and Resilience.

The threat landscape, especially when discussing enterprises, was never moving at a slow pace. But compared to the business email compromise and conventional ransomware attacks of five or 10 years ago, techniques are now evolving faster than ever, meaning insurance agencies must work harder to keep up.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Large language models (LLMs) have enabled threat actors to orchestrate complex attacks, streamline malware and exploit development, design phishing lures without typos, and operate at a scale never before possible. AI introduces uncertainty into threat models built largely around ransomware and data extortion attacks, which insurers have accumulated years of claims data around. Social engineering advancements could alter both attack frequency and severity faster than historical loss data can account for.

While outside of AI, attackers are also coming up with new social engineering tactics all the time, and cloud resource consolidation means compromised credentials or a single stolen API key can lead to devastating consequences.

Thomas Pytel, vice president at Cowbell, tells Dark Reading his firm believes in underwriting that continuously adapts to risk. "AI is changing the speed, scale, and credibility of phishing and impersonation, so historical loss experience alone is insufficient. Underwriting must assess how a business verifies identities, authorizes payments, and controls its own use of AI," he says.

According to a 2025 report from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), cyber insurance premiums reached nearly $15 billion in 2024, up 7% year over year. Additionally, direct written premium (DWP) for the US market reached roughly $9.14 billion in 2024, compared with a market that was only a fraction of that size several years earlier. This underscores how cyber insurance has evolved to become a highly significant segment of the cyber-risk ecosystem.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

On the other hand, that same NAIC report cited nearly 50,000 claims across the US in 2024, the highest on record and a nearly 40% increase year over year. This could speak to the increasing number of customers choosing insurance, the aggressiveness of attackers, or both.

What remains to be seen is whether the industry's growth has outpaced its ability to accurately model the threat landscape.

Increasing insurance popularity also gave way to the rise of certain requirements for coverage, primarily demanding insurance customers uphold a certain quality of cybersecurity posture.

George Gerchow, IANS faculty and chief security officer at Bedrock Data, tells Dark Reading that a few years ago, these requirements were contained on a short form that "no one checked," but insurers now expect multifactor authentication (MFA), endpoint detection and response (EDR), immutable backups, and privileged access controls, while "some are moving to continuous telemetry instead of a once-a-year attestation."

Daniel Woods, head of emerging risks at Coalition, agrees. He says legacy underwriting models based on point-in-time questionnaires cannot keep pace, and this has been true since the ransomware epidemic took hold around 2020.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

This occurred amid concerns that organizations would use cyber insurance as a replacement for patching, practicing defense in depth, or using strong data and authentication controls.

Better posture may be an objective net good no matter where it comes from, though it also risks turning security into a compliance exercise. Gerchow says these requirements can feel like that depending on who you ask.

"Insurance did more to get MFA and EDR deployed in the mid-market than any of us standing on a stage, and that part worked," he says. "But the application is a snapshot, and too many teams treat passing it as the goal. The carrier finds the gap for you at claim time. Lapsed MFA or an untested backup you attested to is now one of the fastest ways to get a claim denied."

Jeremiah Grossman, CEO of cyber loss prevention vendor Root Evidence, says insurance carriers are requiring more to be implemented, steadily, year over year, and "it seems to be working well for many." However, he says, "The issue is that organizations tend to not have the data to properly measure and model their risk, and their carriers are often in a better position to do so."

One relatively recent development in this space has been the rise of insurance organizations as active participants in the security process. While insurers these days broadly require MFA, security products like EDR, managed detection and response (MDR), and validated backups, insurance firms will also offer security products and services directly to their customers.

Coalition's offering includes access to an automated detection and response product, for example, while Resilience offers risk management tooling and Cowbell offers services including risk assessment, penetration testing, and training. All of these firms also work with other security vendors to recommend preapproved products and incident response services. While on the other end, traditional security vendors like Arctic Wolf offer products specifically for insurability.

Coalition argues its "Active Insurance" model has resulted in 73% fewer claims than the industry average and is why 56% of claims reported in 2024 were resolved with no out-of-pocket expense to those insured. Woods says that as the threat landscape intensifies, insurers that passively issue policies and hope claims do not exceed premiums will face increasingly worse results.

"The solution is for insurers to bring threat researchers and security experts in-house to monitor the threat landscape and actively support customers in improving protections during the life cycle of their policies," he says. "Risk transfer is still a fundamental component of cyber insurance, but so is ongoing protection and prevention."

Some risk remains difficult to model. Gerchow argues that if a crisis were to occur tomorrow where a major cloud or identity provider was taken down or compromised, the market would struggle to absorb it, and, he says, "the carriers know it."

"Look at where policy language is moving: war exclusions applied to nation-state activity with no declared conflict, widespread-event carve-outs, and small sublimits for dependent business interruption. CrowdStrike in 2024 was a bad update with no attacker anywhere in it, and it still grounded flights and stalled hospitals in a single morning," he says. "A real compromise of a major identity provider means every downstream customer needs forensics, counsel, and notification at the same time. If I'm a CISO this week, I'm reading the systemic-event exclusions in my policy first and assuming a big piece of that loss stays with me."

#9891. State of Open Models: Summer 2026 Observations

In the AI world, time feels compressed. A few months after our spring report in our biannual analysis worked through the ecosystem, there are quite a few findings that we have observed until this summer. This report lays out these observations from January to August 2026 and presents the data behind each one.

Models and datasets on HF hub are growing on a daily basis. Public model repositories grew from 2.43 to 2.96 million over the period, datasets from 711,000 to 1 million, Spaces from 1.00 to 1.44 million. The distribution underneath stays extreme, roughly 85.6% of models have fewer than 200 lifetime downloads, and 1.5% of repositories account for 99.2% of all downloads. Everything below happens inside that shape.

There used to be a clear progression path: labs would start by releasing smaller models and gradually work their way toward the top end of the scale. In 2026, several Chinese labs skipped this progression entirely.

In almost every month of 2026, the largest and most performant open model from a Chinese lab was larger than any model an American lab released. China's monthly ceiling ran between 754B and 2.78 trillion parameters; U.S. models stayed under 130B in five of seven months, the exception being NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 561B in May and June, and Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab.

The chart splits the labs into two camps. Moonshot, MiniMax, Xiaomi and Z.ai publish almost nothing below 70B, so a developer's first encounter with them is a model too large to run on anything they own. Tencent and Alibaba Qwen cover the whole range instead, from under 1B upward.

Two things made the first camp possible. Building large stopped being a differentiator. Xiaomi, Ant Group and Meituan all cleared a trillion parameters this year, and neither was a household name in open weights twelve months ago. And a lab no longer has to ship a small model to be reachable, because the community's quantization layer will make a large one runnable within days, a dependency we return to below.

That leaves the size profile as a statement of intent rather than of capability. A frontier only portfolio stakes everything on benchmark position and API demand. A full spectrum portfolio is a bid to be the family developers standardise on. Both are rational, they are playing for different prizes.

The United States is not absent from open source.

The two organizations publishing the most new open models this year are also the companies making the hardware: AMD and NVIDIA. Each released more than 200 new model repositories, far ahead of the rest of the field, with LiquidAI ranking third at around 100. Hardware vendors have realized that open models are a way to sell chips: a model optimized for your hardware and freely available is the clearest proof that the hardware works.

When smaller models and embedding models are included, where Google, Microsoft, IBM Granite, and OpenAI’s older vision and speech models generate hundreds of millions of downloads annually, U.S. open source AI is growing.

More hardware and infrastructure organizations such as NVIDIA are training and open-weighting competitive models. NVIDIA's Nemotron model family boasts high performance. Long-time leaders such as Meta reignite open roots with Meta's Muse Glimmer.

At the frontier scale, some U.S. model releases above 100B parameters this year are built on top of Chinese models or leverage artifacts from Chinese labs, such as Thinking Machines’ Inkling (952B). Major original American models include NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Ultra (561B), Nemotron 3 Super (124B), and Arcee AI’s Trinity-Large (399B).

AMD contributed many conversions. This work is important: it enables trillion-parameter models to run efficiently on U.S. hardware. This represents a distribution and optimization layer.

Meanwhile, Chinese open models are increasingly optimized for domestic chips in China, the same competition in reverse, where models are designed around specific hardware ecosystems.

We took the top 25 model repositories by downloads accumulated this year and the top 25 by likes. Exactly one repository appears in both lists.

We counted downloads inside the window rather than lifetime, so nothing is credited for merely having existed longer, and controlling for age makes the split sharper. Not one model published in 2026 reaches the download top 25, while thirteen of the twenty-five date from 2022. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 was pulled 1.55 billion times in seven months against 5,156 likes; Kimi-K3 was pulled about 60 times per like it received.

The two numbers record different acts. A like says a release matters, and goes to frontier models in the weeks after they ship. A download says something is wired into a pipeline that runs on a schedule, and accrues to small, stable models over years. Likes are the right instrument for reading what the field is excited about, downloads for reading what it currently depends on. Treating either as a proxy for the other is the most common mistake we see in coverage of the Hub, including our own earlier work. The same split appears at the level of the publisher.

China's frontier labs are the only accounts on the Hub where the heavy band carries the volume. Effectively all of MiniMax's 2026 downloads are of models above 70B, along with 88% of Moonshot's, 55% of DeepSeek's and 39% of Z.ai's. No large American account looks like this: Google, Microsoft and IBM Granite record essentially none of their 2026 downloads above 70B, and NVIDIA and Meta only 14% and 9%.

The difference becomes clearer in total downloads. Moonshot’s frontier-only portfolio recorded 37M downloads over the year, while Qwen’s broader release strategy across model sizes reached 2,045M (across repositories with declared parameter counts, 2,061M including all repositories) , about 55 times more. The continued expansion of the family, from the 2.4T-parameter Qwen 3.8 Max to smaller variants such as 27B, shows the same focus on coverage across different use cases.

Time also plays an important role. Most models experience a sharp decline in usage after release, followed by a long tail of steady activity. A model’s adoption is largely determined within its first few months.

This helps explain why today’s download volume is often driven not by the newest releases, but by a smaller group of models that have become established infrastructure over time.

If frontier models were a licensing business, you would expect the biggest releases to carry the tightest terms. However, the data below shows a different story.

Of 178 Chinese releases above 20B parameters this year, 59% carry Apache 2.0 and 22% carry MIT, and almost none carry non-commercial restrictions. However, in the last few weeks, we started to see a change on this trend for the really large models, with Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 2.4T starting to include some non-commercial restrictions and revenue share requirements to their licenses

DeepSeek and Z.ai ship models between 700 billion and 1.65 trillion parameters under plain MIT. Chinese labs license their largest models about as permissively as their smallest, and more permissively than American labs license theirs: on the American side of the same size band, 29% is Apache or MIT, 41% sits under custom terms and 30% declares nothing at all.

Whatever these releases are for, it is not licence revenue. The weights are given away on the most permissive terms available. The return has to come from somewhere else: API and cloud business, hardware and platform positioning, or the ecosystem position itself. For instance, the valuations of Z.ai and Kimi point to an effective open source strategy, getting traction and growth opportunities in the community. Going forward, however, the industry is likely to shift toward clearer monetization paths from open-source adoption.

A model’s ecosystem position is not defined only by its own releases, but by how much the community builds on top of it. As mentioned above, Qwen is one exception which is getting attention and adoption.

By this measure, Qwen has become one of the largest foundations in the open model ecosystem. Qwen-based models now account for 151,448 derivatives on the Hub, 2.6× Meta’s total footprint and 4.7× the Llama repositories specifically. Google follows with 82,506 derivatives. The third-largest source is Unsloth, a community account publishing quantized and fine-tuning-ready builds, many of which further extend the Qwen ecosystem.

Qwen derivatives have increased at roughly 180–210 new repositories per day throughout the first seven months of 2026, showing that adoption is not driven only by individual launches. Qwen has become part of the default workflow for developers deciding what models to fine-tune and deploy.

Several factors contributed to this position. First, consistency. Qwen has maintained a regular release cadence, continuously updating its model family rather than relying on occasional flagship releases. Second, coverage. It publishes models across a wide range of sizes and use cases, allowing developers to stay within the same ecosystem whether they need a small local model or a larger deployment model. Third, openness. Apache 2.0 licensing reduces friction for modification, redistribution, and commercial use.

These factors reinforce each other. A broad model family attracts more developers; more developers create more derivatives; and those derivatives make the ecosystem more attractive to future users.

This position was built largely by the community. The 151,448 derivatives represent downstream work created by other developers, not releases produced by Qwen itself. Even among the 28,531 GGUF conversions of Qwen models on the Hub, Qwen published only 54.

Among models that declare a parameter count, those under 1B take 83% of all-time downloads and everything above 100B takes 1%. Restricting to downloads accumulated in 2026 changes nothing: 3% of the volume goes to models above 70B. This is the March finding that has held up most cleanly, for the same reason as before, small models are the only ones that run on the hardware most developers actually have.

So how does a trillion-parameter model reach anyone at all? Through llama.cpp.

In February the ggml team joined Hugging Face, with the project remaining fully open-source, community-governed and in the same technical direction. What changed is that the most important project in local inference now has durable resources behind it.

The ceiling moved with llama.cpp. The July snapshot carries GGUF builds of DeepSeek-V4-Flash at roughly 284B parameters and Kimi-K3 at roughly 2.8 trillion. Local inference used to mean an 8B model on a laptop. It now means a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts spread across a few consumer machines, which is the alternative route the frontier did not have a year ago, and the reason a frontier-first release strategy is viable at all.

And that route runs on Qwen: 39.6 million GGUF downloads a month, nearly twice Gemma's 20.8 million and more than five times Llama's 7.5 million. The Llama gap is not a supply problem, Llama-derived GGUF repositories slightly outnumber Qwen's. Same shelf space, a fifth of the traffic.

Model repositories grew 21.5% over these seven months. Several things around them grew several times faster.

Repositories declaring the gguf library rose 464%, lerobot 194% and Apple's mlx148%, against 16% for transformers and peft and 21% for diffusers. The modelling core is growing at roughly the platform average. The layer that decides where a model can physically run local inference formats, Apple silicon, robot control stacks, is growing three to seven times faster than that.

Across the ten largest model families, the labs behind these models publish very few official GGUF conversions. Yet GGUF versions are often the ones used by developers running models locally. Providing an official conversion at release, documenting quantization choices, and signing the artifacts would require limited additional effort. Rather than maintaining this workflow internally, labs could collaborate with existing ecosystem contributors such as Unsloth. Doing so would narrow the gap between the weights tested by model creators and the versions adopted by the broader community.

We could not have written this section in March, because the instrument did not exist. The agent-usage dataset, published in July, records the agent/ token that coding agents send when they call the Hub through huggingface_hub or the hf CLI — searching for models, pushing datasets, running Jobs, creating Spaces. For the first time we can see how much agent traffic the Hub receives and which harnesses it comes from.

Claude Code led July with 44.4%, but a single month conceals the real finding: it held 67.8% in April and 64% in May, while Codex climbed steadily from 10.4% to 20.8%. This is a market with no incumbent, where one release or one changed default can move half the traffic in a month.

The second finding is the unregistered row. Nearly a quarter of agent-tagged traffic in July came from harnesses not yet named in the dataset, and in May that figure was 59.8%. Between April and July more than a dozen new client identifiers appeared. New entrants are arriving faster than any registry can name them — which is itself the finding.

We spent much of the year building for this reader rather than only for human browsers. Papers began serving machine-readable Markdown in March. April brought agent traces as a first-class dataset type and an agents.md endpoint on every Gradio Space, so an agent can read a Space's API and call it directly. July brought the hf_fs tool on our MCP server, exposing repositories, storage, docs and papers through a single interface in just over a thousand tokens, alongside attachable sandboxes for secure execution. The same consolidation happened at the protocol layer, with MCP moving into the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

Then, in July, an agent stopped being a reader and became an intruder. What appears to be the first documented case of an autonomous agent running a sustained intrusion on its own initiative happened to us. While our team tried to use frontier closed models to analyze the captured attack code, their safety guardrails declined the work. The analysis was completed in the end on a quantized open model GLM-5.2 running on our own infrastructure. We published a disclosure and a full technical timeline.

Compared to the spring report, the geographical rebalancing of power continues to accelerate. While U.S. open source models continue to be competitive, the race between several Chinese frontier model labs draws strong attention. Many likes on these frontier models point to what excites the community the most, and growth opportunity for companies leveraging the attention for valuations.

However, the AI race is not only sprints, but also a marathon; tools like llama.cpp helps deploying the big models locally, but a broad model family and its adoption is still the key, to build a positive feedback loop between developers, publisher and future users. Models to be embedded in the infrastructure and being part of the ecosystem, may lead to a commercially sound exit at the end of the tunnel.

In the end, with agents being the number 1 user on HF Hub for the first time, the next report may look very different.

In AI, a few months can reshape the ecosystem.

This analysis is based on activity observed on the Hugging Face Hub during the first seven months of 2026.

The metrics used in this report, including downloads, likes, derivatives, and model releases, represent different aspects of ecosystem activity. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of model quality, commercial adoption, or overall market share.

Downloads indicate usage within the Hub ecosystem, but they do not capture API usage, private deployments, or models distributed through other channels.

Likes reflect community attention and interest, while derivative models provide a signal of how much developers build on top of an existing model.

Because open-source AI adoption happens across many channels, Hub activity should be viewed as one perspective on ecosystem development rather than a complete measurement of the AI market.

This article was edited to include latest releases in early August.

#9890. Why Caribbean Threats Cascade Into Global Cyber-Risk

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The region is demonstrating what happens when exploits accelerate but assurance does not.

On July 24, 2025, Curaçao's Tax and Customs Administration found ransomware on its network. Counter services, the call center, and internal processes went dark for more than a week, and the island's recovery depended on specialists flown in from the Netherlands.

A day earlier, the Joint Court of Justice had gone down as well. Because that court serves Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, Bonaire, Saba, and Sint Eustatius, a single intrusion degraded the judicial system of six jurisdictions at once.

That is the Caribbean's defining security characteristic, and it is why the interval between an exposure appearing and an exposure closing matters more here than almost anywhere else.

Consider what that interval currently is.

Fortinet's "Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition" recorded roughly 325 million attack attempts across the English-speaking Caribbean in 2025, an extraordinary volume against a small economic base, with critical vulnerabilities now targeted within 24 to 48 hours of disclosure, down from an average of nearly five days.

Related:Nigeria Deepens Cybersecurity Efforts as Cybercriminals See More Profits

IBM's 2026 "Cost of a Data Breach Report" puts the mean time to identify and contain a breach at 247 days, up 2.5% and reversing five consecutive years of improvement.

Both of those numbers moved this year, and they moved in opposite directions. Exploitation got faster. Finding and containing it got slower, for the first time in five years.

Here is the part that the security industry has not absorbed: third-party assurance still runs on an annual cycle. A global insurer assesses its Caribbean claims processor once a year.

A hotel chain reviews its regional franchisee's controls at renewal. A correspondent bank collects an attestation and files it. Every one of those instruments is calibrated to a threat landscape that stopped existing several years ago.

The questionnaire signed in March describes a network that was materially different by April and unrecognizable by October. Twelve months of assurance against 48 hours of exposure, and nobody has repriced the difference.

That mismatch is not a Caribbean failing. It is a global control design failing, and the Caribbean is simply where it shows up first because of what sits inside the interval.

The plumbing is ordinary. A business process outsourcer holds live credentials into a North American insurer's claims platform. A hotel group's property management system federates to a global loyalty program. A regional bank sits inside correspondent rails that clear in New York. An attacker who compromises the small end inherits trust at the large end, and does it inside a window where the large end's assurance process has no way to notice.

Related:Mexico's New Cyber Plan Faces Its First Real Test

The obvious response is that Caribbean organizations should simply patch faster.

Having spent two decades running security operations across these markets, I can tell you why that answer keeps failing. Security teams here are frequently two or three people covering an entire institution.

Critical systems often cannot be taken offline because there is no redundant capacity to fail over to. Vendor support is remote and time-zoned away. And where six jurisdictions share one platform, no single institution can authorize a maintenance window on it.

These are structural constraints, not attitudes, and telling the region to try harder has not moved the number in years.

Measure remediation against exploit velocity, not the audit calendar. Report critical MTTR as a distribution against a 48-hour benchmark. An average conceals the tail, and the tail is where the exposure lives.

Replace annual attestations with continuous evidence. If your assurance over a supplier is a document signed in March, you are not managing that risk; you're recording that you once looked at it.

Assume some things can't be patched in time, and design for that. Segmentation, compensating controls, and explicit, owned, time-boxed decisions about what stays exposed. An undocumented exception is the same as no control.

Instrument the federated paths, not just the perimeter. Stolen credentials remain the primary route into cloud environments, and federated access is where a stolen credential stops being your incident and becomes your partner's.

Assess the shared provider, not just the institution. Where multiple entities run on one platform, assessing each separately measures the same risk repeatedly and reduces it once, at best.

The Caribbean isn't asking for allowances. It is showing the rest of the industry, early and in public, what happens when exploitation accelerates and assurance does not.

Anyone whose supply chain touches this region is measuring a snapshot of a system that has already changed.

Marlon Cooper is CEO of Symptai Consulting and Group Head of Managed Security Services for Digicel Business, with oversight of security operations across the English-speaking Caribbean.

#9888. Burnt TOAST

Postgres at AI speed — deploy anywhere. Explore pgEdge Starfleet →

A financial firm hired me in 2010 to revise their Postgres cluster architecture. During my stint there, I learned a healthy respect for their event_log table. But perhaps “respect” is the wrong word here, as it was more of a deep loathing. This table, you see, was the canonical ledger of system events and consisted of several million rows.

The high row count wasn’t a problem by itself. We kept a tight visibility window and archived frequently. Unfortunately for us, one of the columns was an unconstrained TEXT type that commonly held a large blob of XML. Thus any fetch from this table was inordinately slow. Writing was equally painful. We went through great pains to shape the application itself to avoid touching it except when absolutely necessary. It was evil incarnate.

The performance of this table initially confused and enraged me—until I remembered about TOAST. Postgres likes to innocuously dub this backronym “The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique” but DBAs in the field maintain a love/hate relationship with the system. Whether that’s justified is a different question.

On the surface, it’s a way to store huge blocks of data elsewhere to keep tuples small and avoid exceeding the relatively petite 8KB data page size. Postgres creates a shadow table for the bulky content, splits it up into chunks, and stores a pointer in the original row. It’s an elegant solution to a pressing issue, but there are deep performance implications.

So let’s dig into precisely why DBAs secretly dread large text-based columns, shall we?

To really understand what happened in my event_log case, it’s good to reconstruct some semblance of it.

And then we can bootstrap the table with 100k rows. Just enough to make it annoying! The data column needs to be big, but not absolutely gigantic. Let’s start with up to 1000 data points:

Great! Now where did all of that data go? If you thought, “Into the event_log table of course!” you’re wrong. Instead, Postgres helpfully created a TOAST table for most of it. Let’s check the pg_class catalog for the other objects:

That’s three objects for the price of one: the original table, a toast table, and a toast table index. This doesn’t always happen, but if your table has a text-like column without a maximum length, it probably did. In this case, it’s because an unbounded JSON column can contain anything, so Postgres preemptively initialized a TOAST table to store the “anything”.

What goes in is a bit more subtle, and is where the trouble starts brewing.

There’s a kind of inherent hierarchy that determines how data gets managed. The typstorage column in the pg_type catalog explains how this works for each type Postgres understands. There are four valid storage methods:

PLAIN (p): The value stays inline and uncompressed. This is the default for fixed-width types like INT and TIMESTAMPTZ.

MAIN (m): Compression is allowed, with TOAST only as the last resort. The default for NUMERIC.

EXTERNAL (e): TOAST is allowed, but compression is not.

EXTENDED (x): Anything is fair game. This is the default for TEXT, BYTEA, JSONB, and most other variable-length types.

Postgres imposes a loop on all text-based column types in a tuple that it applies until the entire row is under the standard 8KB page threshold (minus overhead). It looks something like this:

Being the default for JSON, all of our data follows the rules for EXTENDED. We can see it in action by checking a few rows:

The toast_tuple_target storage setting tells Postgres when to toast column contents. The default is around 2KB of compressed data, and anything after that is moved into TOAST automatically. The example above has a row that compresses right under that limit, and as a result, never gets moved.

If we examine page 57 specifically, this becomes even more clear:

The tuple size of the rows that didn’t get toasted is much larger than those that did. That’s thanks to a pointer replacing the toasted values. And that’s not all. Toasted data is also broken into chunks. Every toasted value gets broken into 1996-byte blocks and stored in sequential order as rows in the toast table.

Any toasted value implies at least one fetch from the toast table. That’s a read on the toast index and a read on the toast table itself per chunk.

Chunks must be re-assembled. That’s extra memory usage and can be significant depending on chunk count.

Compressed data must also be decompressed. That’s both memory and CPU overhead.

The intuitive read of this is that TOAST is always worse. But is it?

Let’s run an experiment! We already have a table where some of the data is toasted. What happens if we force Postgres to select all of it?

This requires some setup. To begin, we create a non-toasted table by setting the event_data column to use MAIN storage. That allows it to be compressed, but not toasted unless the full tuple exceeds a Postgres page size. Like so:

Then we can directly compare the costs of pulling out field 999 from the data:

Take a look at that! Shared buffers really saved our bacon on this one. Total buffer reads on the toasted column required 288127 total reads versus 40754 for the non-toasted version. Conversely, the toasted table is much smaller:

While Postgres can read through the heap faster, it then has to spend a lot of time seeking through the toast table. This size difference translates to some non-intuitive behavior. For instance, most interactions with the toasted table are actually much faster. Consider counting all rows:

That’s 26ms vs 91ms. Or jumping through offsets:

Any time Postgres has to deal directly with the heap, performance suffers immensely. Toast pointers can act as an optimization, particularly when not interacting with the toasted column because they make each row on the heap much smaller.

This one kind of blew my mind. It turns out that the problem with the event_log table wasn’t necessarily the TOAST system, but the event_data column itself. It turns out there’s a way to fix that.

Back then, “fixing that” meant to split the table. Our toy example is a mere 100k rows, but the real one was several million and the heap alone was over 1GB. Including TOAST on those huge XML blobs brought the total table size to over 20GB.

When an application is full of SELECT * and is repeatedly looking up and decoding toasted data, it can eventually take a toll. Even if we ignore the disk IO, that’s a lot of extra network bandwidth. “Just specify the column names!” you might say, and I agree. If only it were that easy to modify ORM-generated queries and five years of accumulated hand-written ones.

What do we gain from this? For one, we no longer need to carry around the TOAST pointers in the main application table. Secondly, since this column was a mix of toasted and non-toasted values due to the toast_tuple_target cutoff, even non-toasted values have been relocated. We can see this in the new table heap sizes:

All operations will now be substantially faster simply because page density is now guaranteed to be higher. More rows fit on each page, and there are fewer pages required to represent the primary core of the table. The entire heap is now 5MB rather than 47MB, a saving of over 9x. If it’s at all possible to relocate large columns to an optional JOIN in a high-performance system, it may be worth taking a second look.

If you think we could have achieved a similar effect by setting toast_tuple_target arbitrarily low, think again. The TOAST system won’t even activate if a row value is shorter than TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD, a compiled value that acts as a hard minimum. Values below this won’t even be considered for toasting. What can I say? Postgres is a picky eater.

The obvious objection is that applications now need a join. Well, the Postgres planner has you covered:

The trick is the LEFT JOIN, making the event data optional even though we know every row has a value there. Queries that don’t specify the column will prune the JOIN and everyone is happy.

As of Postgres 14, it’s even possible to choose the compression type. Stick with the venerable built-in pglz, or use lz4 if it’s been compiled into your binaries. The default for the entire server comes from default_toast_compression:

Or it can be set using the COMPRESSION decorator during CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE.

One interesting note about the compression types is that pglz is somewhat quirky. It skips values under 32 bytes, demands at least 25% savings, and gives up entirely if it finds nothing to compress in the first 1KB. The last rule is kind of odd to see in action:

There are also some associated performance implications. Consider:

When dealing with 100k rows of 10k compressed values, lz4 is a bit slower decompressing by about 20% in this case, but is over 30 times faster at compression. That’s absolutely staggering.

Look, we all want to play the blame game. I always blamed the TOAST system for how badly our application’s event_log table performed. Every time someone complained. Any occasion when a badly written query made it through the application and touched the table in a way that apparently enraged it and caused every page load to quadruple or time out entirely. In my head, TOAST was at fault.

Ironically, it was TOAST’s fault in a way, because it’s not aggressive enough. Think about it. Postgres needs TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD to avoid activating the expensive machinery that deconstructs, compresses, and moves data to an external table. But imagine how things could look if anything could be offloaded arbitrarily. Unfortunately there’s no option for that. Out of PLAIN, MAIN, EXTENDED, and EXTERNAL, none cover the case for “move anything over 100 bytes and also compress it if it’s over 2k.” Though there’s an argument for using EXTERNAL on medium-sized but “large-ish” columns: we gain the benefit of a smaller heap, and data less than 1kb doesn’t tend to compress well anyway.

Instead, we have to compromise our schema design and introduce an extra join for parts of the application that actually interact with the bulky column. Views sidestep this to an extent, but it’s something of an ugly hack compared to leaving the table intact. We also can’t leverage this maneuver every single time a big column shows up, or our schema would end up a horrifying mess. Not all columns are “optional” enough to banish.

What TOAST provides is a suitable middle-ground. For the cost of a pointer, we get to essentially forget a huge block of text exists in the table at all. The heap is happier and we’re none the wiser. Compression speeds are also dramatically faster for those who switch to lz4.

So don’t be afraid of Postgres TOAST; it’s the best kind there is.
