#9864. How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

For Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:

The expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:

Our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 new features:

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Our corpus build starts by exporting the latest version of every paper from a repeatable-read PostgreSQL snapshot. The exporter streams rows rather than loading the catalog into memory, writes bounded JSONL shards, and creates a manifest containing row counts and SHA-256 checksums.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

Only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:

If the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can quickly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

The revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

Scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

New generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

#9863. So Many AI Security Benchmarks, but None Tell the Whole Story

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Measuring artificial intelligence model security gets complex, fast, thanks to a growing patchwork of benchmarks targeting different variables in the equation. But none replace testing against your own code and workflows.

Cybersecurity firms and the makers of foundational models are improving the performance and efficiency of their artificial intelligence (AI) systems. But quantifying that performance improvement is a challenge.

While claims of more efficient models with smaller token costs arrive every week, gauging whether those models perform as well as the more general-purpose members of an AI model's family remains difficult. The lesson for organizations: Test models against your code and workflows to make the best choice for your business requirements.

National sovereign AI and cyber-defense firm Dream Group, for example, used 220,000 vulnerability records, threat intelligence reports, detection rules, and other cybersecurity documents to train an 8 billion parameter model — among the smallest modern models — to perform efficiently on cybersecurity tasks. The model — dubbed the Mid-trained Security Transformer (MiST) — improved average performance across 13 cybersecurity tasks, consisting mainly of multiple-choice and true-false questions about vulnerability analysis and cybersecurity domains.

Related:L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara

The results show that stronger security capabilities do not necessarily need a more complex model; more specialized training and adding better software around the model both improve results, says Elad Ben Zaken, an AI researcher at Dream Group.

"I expect efficiency to keep improving in coding and security tasks through specialization and better workflows," he says. "The model supplies capability; the harness determines how effectively it uses context and tools. Adding more of either can increase cost without improving results."

Dream is not alone in finding ways to make models more efficient. When Anthropic released Opus 5.5 in September, for example, the company said that the model improved performance while costing 40% less than Opus 5 on "typical workloads."

However, for cybersecurity tasks, very little is typical. One model's results may mean little to companies looking for an expert system to generate secure code or to effectively find weaknesses in the enterprise's attack surface. On the offensive side, researchers are creating their own benchmarks to measure the performance of cybersecurity-focused models.

For offensive-security firm XBOW, the metrics that matter concern the ability to find and exploit vulnerabilities. Because different customers may want to use specific models, the company creates its own harness to improve outcomes regardless of the model used, says Albert Ziegler, head of AI at XBOW. While other organizations may want to use AI to analyze defensive telemetry and signals to boost detection of potential attacks, XBOW's metrics focus on finding vulnerabilities and exploit chains.

Related:Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

"In its most atomic form, that's the ability of the model to find an exploit — that is our bread and butter in terms of seeing what's the value that the model produces," Ziegler says. "For other companies, this bread and butter could obviously be something else."

Anthropic's Opus 5 Thinking leads the board on one metric, correctness, among large language models. Source: Sonar's LLM Leaderboard

Another benchmark, the SEC-Bench Pro, attempts to measure an AI agent's ability to independently rediscover and trigger a known memory-safety bug in a browser engine or the Linux kernel, but only after the general location and type of bug are specified. Created by a research team at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, the metric ranks Codex and GPT-5.5 as the current favorites, with an overall solve rate of 58%. It also finds that open-weight models tend to struggle, with GLM-5 only succeeding in 13 of the 344 test cases.

Other metrics measure the hacking capabilities of AI models over an entire attack chain. Government contractor Booz Allen, for example, has published its Cyber Weapons Index (CWI), which combines a model's ability to find and exploit vulnerabilities with its effectiveness at executing attacks on a target. The latest version of the list puts OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on top with a CWI of 80.5, just edging out Claude Mythos with a score of 80.

Related:Ransomware Gangs Embrace Physical Threats, Family Stalking?

"The CWI offers one empirical approach to offensive cyber capability — test models against a common enterprise network and score demonstrated actions using network evidence, rather than relying on what models say they can do," says Eric Syphard, senior vice president and head of AI at Booz Allen. "There is no single measure that captures every security risk. Evaluations need to be designed around the capability being assessed and should make their methods, environment, and success criteria clear."

Similarly, the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) continues to benchmark the capabilities of AI models to complete a 32-step attack chain. So far, two models can: Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview and OpenAI GPT 5.5.

In their own research, Dream researchers found that expert curation of a primary knowledge database — a "seed corpus" — can be used to create domain-specific synthetic training data, thus avoiding relying on general knowledge databases for training specialized models. The latest MiST models, MiST-8B and MiST-30B-A3B, were evaluated using 13 different test datasets, including 1,072 multiple-choice questions about MITRE ATT&CK (SECURE-MAET) and 870 true-false questions about whether a particular piece of code is vulnerable (the PrimeVul P-C).

Overall, the various features, capabilities, and issues are hard to benchmark in any comprehensive way. While offensive security metrics and measurements of defensive capabilities are both evolving quickly, other areas — such as safety — are more difficult to benchmark. The AISI found that the most sophisticated models tend to execute unwanted actions, such as OpenAI's GPT Astra conducting unsanctioned supply chain attacks, but overall safety measurements are more anecdotal than comprehensive.

Creating a metric for a model's likelihood of taking unwanted actions, for example, is very difficult, XBOW's Ziegler says.

"Benchmarking the possibility of the model to do harm is incredibly hard," he says. "You run [the test case for the model] 1,000 times, and it doesn't do any harm, and then you run it the 1,001 time, it drops your database. That 1,001 time negates all the first thousand runs that went well."

In addition, just because a model is newer does not mean it's more secure or has more advanced security capabilities, says Joe Tyler, general manager and AI researcher at Sonar, a provider of AI code verification and governance tools. The company regularly runs the latest large language models (LLMs) through a testing pipeline to generate scores across a series of benchmarks — from cognitive complexity to vulnerability occurrence in its code — which it then posts to its LLM Leaderboard for Code Quality & Security.

The ranking can give companies a general sense of model performance, but it should only be the starting point for companies evaluating LLM security performance, Tyler says. Instead, organizations should tailor their test pipelines to their own situations.

"Start with the task and the failures you can't accept, rather than assuming the newest model is the right choice," he says. "Public benchmarks help shortlist candidates, but the decision needs evaluations that reflect your own code and workflows."

In addition, for most organizations the choice of model may be constrained by the technology platforms they've adopted. For that reason, security teams should not necessarily focus on selecting specific models but instead seek out AI-powered services that lead to more efficiency, better coverage, and faster response.

Attackers' adoption of AI means companies will need to deal with a greater influx of vulnerabilities and faster time to exploitation, says Nico Waisman, XBOW's CISO. As a result, organizations should invest in tools and processes that help security teams move faster, automate repetitive work, and reduce the time to remediation. Focus on the impact of AI-based solutions, not their raw benchmarks, he says.

"Ultimately, I wouldn't evaluate AI security tools based on which model they use or how impressive their demos look," Waisman says. "I would evaluate them based on measurable outcomes: Are they helping you identify real risks? Are they reducing your exposure? Are they making your team significantly faster? That's where the security budget should go."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9861. C++26 Disapproved

On October 23, 2026, the unthinkable happened. It was supposed to be a mere formality: C++26 was up for a vote by the ISO National Bodies (NBs). The options are always approval, rejection, or abstention. Comments are also allowed. Since 1998, this process had run quietly and smoothly. Not so on October 23, 2026. After a twelve-week voting period, the result is in: Disapproved!

I would like to mention here that I am a member of the C++ Standardization Committee and, together with my colleagues, represent Germany’s vote. ISO rules also stipulate that certain votes are internal to ISO, and the results—or the breakdown of the results—may not be published. This article contains my own personal views.

As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of C++ that DIS ballot failed. When I searched the ISO system, I could only find one other DIS that was not approved: ISO/IEC DIS 26926 C++/CLI Language Specification dated August 11, 2006. It’s possible that my search privileges aren’t sufficient to view everything, but all ISO programming languages should be visible to me. The sad end of ISO/IEC DIS 26926: the project was halted. I mention this upfront to clarify the significance of this vote.

In the following, I will use various terms from everyday ISO terminology. At https://isocpp.org/std/iso-iec-jtc1-procedures, there is an overview of the various stages of an ISO standard. DIS is the penultimate stage. As the overview also shows, a two-thirds majority is required. This majority was not achieved.

The reason for the rejection is quite clear from the comments submitted by the National Bodies (NBs): contracts. Put simply, a number of NBs believe that this feature is not yet ready for release.

Now it gets complicated. The C++ Standardization Committee, also known as WG21, follows ISO rules but also has some additional rules. One of these is (or was) that opinions are always heard whenever new information becomes available. If an opinion was heard and a feature was nevertheless not changed as desired, the person respects the outcome and accepts that many others disagree.

However, the voting body at the NB level may also consist of other individuals, or the NBs are, of course, free to vote differently.

The previous practice was that NBs would only vote against a standard if new information became available or if errors in the process or similar issues were identified. This changed on October 23, 2026.

It’s difficult to judge in this complex situation; the NBs who want C++26 without Contracts argue that there is new information. I myself find it hard to share this view. A new paper with old arguments is not new information to me.

The feature has been on the wish list for a long time. I was already in the room in Cologne back in 2019, at the time for C++20, when Contracts, in a different form back then, were being included in the standard. I was also in the room when the feature was removed from C++20 again during the same meeting. As a result, a study group was formed to address the topic of Contracts and its various aspects from 2020 to approximately 2024. Afterward, the study group submitted its work and proposals to the Evolution Working Group (EWG), the central body for language extensions. There, the topic was discussed further over several meetings before being included in C++26 by a majority vote.

In the next step, WG21 voted on the C++26 draft in March 2026, which included Contracts. Here, too, a large majority was achieved, though not without dissenting votes.

And that brings us to the next phase: DIS. At this stage, there were enough “no” votes that a two-thirds majority was not reached.

The big problem: what happens next? ISO, of course, has a process for this. It offers various options:

All of these possibilities mean a delay in the next C++ standard. Whether it will still be called C++26 is also up in the air, but that’s a much smaller issue.

The difficulty with all four options is that they require a majority within WG21. However, this working group voted to move C++26 with Contracts into the next voting phase leading to its release. And it did so with more than just the required two-thirds majority. The feature didn’t come out of nowhere, either; it was developed over the course of years through the work and possibly personal commitment of many people. It’s hard to imagine that this group would simply want to abandon its work, which has received approval on multiple occasions so far. The same applies to the group that is dissatisfied with Contracts. This group, too, has invested effort, in some cases even in alternative implementations. It’s hard to imagine that, after these groups voted “no” in the DIS vote, the result would change without Contracts being removed.

Even the last option removing C++26 requires a majority in WG21. As I understand it, this step would mean reverting to C++23 and proceeding to C++29 without a single change. This would affect the work of even more people. WG21 would then be tasked with incorporating features that have already been successfully included in C++26 into C++29. Since this can only be done through a paper backed by at least one person advocating for it, features could be omitted if that person lacks the motivation or time.

Of course, certainty about the voting outcome can only be achieved if the respective path is actually taken.

Unfortunately, the way forward is currently more than uncertain. Perhaps this also explains why ISO/IEC DIS 26926 marked the end of this activity. Consensus is needed to move forward. Trust is always required for consensus. Unfortunately, that trust has just been shaken.

The next C++ standard, and thus the future of C++, is currently at an impasse.

The good news is that the next meeting will take place on November 16, which is just a few days away. The top priority will be to break the deadlock. This will very likely have implications for C++29 as well; in fact, there is currently no reason to continue working on this project.

Normally, my articles are technically focused and free of personal opinion. Regarding the rejected DIS, I can only say that I consider it a massive disaster and feel sorry for the entire C++ community. Regardless of whether someone likes Contracts, considers them important, or sees major weaknesses in them, the topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting “no,” an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken. Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes. Overall, the result is one in which all participants have given their best. During the DIS vote, the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust.

#9860. 'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

The malware's focus on AI tools expands the traditional infostealer playbook to expose a forest of AI sessions, sensitive business data, and developer infrastructure from a single compromised endpoint.

A novel infostealer that specifically targets AI applications and development tools is changing the narrative on illicit data monetization, opening up fresh revenue streams through extortion and other abuses of the stolen data.

Researchers from Check Point Software discovered the malware, dubbed Aokigahara after the Japanese "haunted forest" at the base of Mount Fuji, which does typical stealer things, they said in a recent report. It targets Windows-based machines and the browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications running on them — among other apps and services — with data theft.

However, Aokigahara is notable in that it has a particular focus on emerging AI-driven assets, collecting authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools, according to Check Point. This sets it apart from many of the infostealers currently active in the wild.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

"This expanded targeting reflects a broader shift in what attackers may consider valuable, not only personal accounts and financial data but also access to AI services and the environments developers use to build software," according to Check Point.

The AI data offers unique opportunities for threat actors to benefit financially from the stealer's activities by using credentials or session tokens to "enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts," according to the report.

The malicious activity can also extend to developer and cloud environments, and thus threaten enterprises. Indeed, threat actors have already demonstrated how they use stolen credentials for GitHub accounts, SSH private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credential and configuration files to infiltrate cloud environments of enterprise targets.

This may also pave the way for extortion of organizations by holding stolen data for ransom, according to Check Point.

"Users can share sensitive business information, proprietary source code, and other confidential material with AI services," according to the post. "If stolen credentials or session tokens provide access to conversation histories or uploaded files, attackers could potentially threaten to disclose that information to demand payment."

Denis Calderone, chief technology officer of security firm Suzu Labs, tells Dark Reading that "stolen AI credentials can yield a heavy harvest for an attacker. A paid AI subscription is a resellable asset, and the conversation history behind it is often full of proprietary code, which means these stolen sessions now carry extortion value alongside their resale value."

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

Other targeted data the malware looks for are developer and cloud credentials, including Git access data, SSH keys, and configuration files for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. This data is valuable to give attackers access to private code repositories or cloud resources if the stolen credentials remain valid and have sufficient permissions, according to Check Point.

Indeed, "a developer's AI assistant is a keyring," Calderone observes, and some of those keys ultimately could give attackers access to the kingdom.

"The same malware that lifts the Cursor or Copilot session is also grabbing Git credentials, SSH private keys, and AWS config files off that workstation, so one infected machine can expose the codebase, the repos, and the cloud in a single run," he says.

Related:EDR Evasion Stack Helps Process Injection Slip Past Defenses

Aokigahara also has built-in anti-detection mechanisms. It checks for analysis environments such as virtual machines and sandboxes, and packages stolen data into zip archives and then encrypts it before sending it to attacker-controlled servers.

Aokigahara's targeting of AI tools expands the traditional infostealer playbook, potentially exposing AI sessions, sensitive business data, and developer infrastructure from a single compromised endpoint. The theft of this data then opens new pathways for financial gain for attackers and thus may provide an incentive for others to do the same, according to Check Point.

This means that defenders should start treating AI-tool authentication data as enterprise secrets, with protections comparable to those applied to cloud credentials and developer keys. To that end, security teams should hunt for AI-session theft by investigating suspicious access to local application storage and authentication-related files belonging to AI assistants, coding agents, and developer IDEs.

Organizations also should more closely protect developer and cloud credentials by reducing the persistence of long-lived secrets on endpoints, using managed identity and short-lived credentials where feasible, and restricting access to cloud resources and source-code repositories.

Further, organizations can protect assets across exposed apps and tools by revoking exposed sessions and rotating secrets. If an endpoint is suspected of compromise, according to Check Point, they should assess AI sessions, API keys, GitHub credentials, SSH keys, and cloud tokens, not just browser passwords.

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9859. Wire It, Run It, Deploy It: AI Workflows in Gradio

Most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something new. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

The best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

One graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

Since this is a workflow, each of the three outputs also gets its own REST endpoint: /sticker, /voiceover, and /episode_title. You can call any of them directly from code without opening the UI. See Call it from code below for a runnable example.

Type in one idea, and it turns into a set of generated artwork all at once: a base image from FLUX, two AI re-imaginings of that image (a soft watercolor version and a neon cyberpunk take), and a gallery title written by an LLM.

Each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

You get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

Every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

Decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

Check out this demo that animates a still image using Lightricks/LTX-Video loaded through Diffusers, running entirely through one node. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know anything about your GPU setup. It simply calls the bound function.

Every workflow is a graph with three kinds of nodes: references (your inputs), operators (the steps that do work), and subjects (your outputs). An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

Every workflow you build is also an API, with no extra work. Each output becomes a REST endpoint named after its label, and you can call it from Python with the Gradio client. Here is a live, no-token example against the multi-endpoint demo Space, exactly as-is:

Endpoints that call a model or a Space run under a Hugging Face token, so pass one when you create the client:

Prefer plain HTTP? Every endpoint is reachable over curl too:

For the full walkthrough, the operator kinds, the JSON schema, and reusable patterns, see the official gr.Workflow guide in the Gradio docs.

You can even build something as involved as AUTOMATIC1111 with gr.Workflow. Keep an eye out for our next post, where we walk through building it step by step. Here is a sneak peek 😉👇

#9858. Beware the Slasher: AI Could Kill Off Cybersecurity Pros' Skills

Nathan Hamiel outlines potential SecOps horror in the AI midst, as core technical capabilities go the way of reading an atlas or remembering phone numbers.

Black Hat India — Bengaluru — The use of AI as a tool to enhance cybersecurity operations is emerging as a double-edged knife for security professionals. While it can make them more capable, it could also spell the demise of the very skills they need to use it effectively.

That's the concern of Nathan Hamiel, senior director of research at Kudelski Security, who has made a case for how evolving technology can erode technical skills since well before the generative AI boom. Now, that concern is getting much louder.

Speaking to Dark Reading recently, he says he began noticing the problem around 2005 and 2006, when he encountered cybersecurity professionals who lacked a firm grasp of the fundamentals of their work. At that time, he warned about the dangers of relying too heavily on various types of technical tools, declaring to cybersecurity professionals that "your tools are killing you," and warning that practitioners are moving away from being "hands-on" operators who investigate problems directly, and toward "hands-off" monitors who oversee results presented through tools, interfaces, and dashboards.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

It's a shift that's being exacerbated now by AI-driven automation, he says, and organizations need to move quickly to optimize the use of AI without the expense of cybersecurity skill-building.

While automation can simplify complex tasks and allow professionals to accomplish more, it can also distance them from the underlying problems they are trying to solve. Without a solid understanding of the fundamentals, practitioners may struggle to recognize when a tool produces an incorrect result or when its findings require further investigation, Hamiel says.

"We need to keep these skills and not let them degrade because those skills are important to making the tools work in the best way possible," he tells Dark Reading from this week's Black Hat India conference, where he's giving a keynote entitled "The Death of Skills and the Persistence of Problems."

"What AI adds to somebody with knowledge and experience is some additional capabilities," Hamiel elaborates. "A domain expert wielding AI is going to be able to gain benefits from using that tool that a novice with no domain experience isn't going to be able to get."

This distinction is becoming increasingly important as AI becomes more deeply integrated into cybersecurity workflows. It also raises questions about how the industry will develop its next generation of experts if automation removes some of the hands-on tasks that junior professionals traditionally learn.

Related:Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit

The current discussion around AI often falls into extremes, Hamiel says. Some predict that the technology can go a long way toward solving major problems facing not only cybersecurity but also humanity, while others warn that it will bring the industry — and some even the world — to an end.

"You have the doomers," he says, "and you have people who say this is a big nothingburger. The truth is somewhere in the middle."

For Hamiel, understanding AI's impact requires separating what the technology can demonstrate in a controlled environment from what it can reliably accomplish in the real world. Impressive capabilities do not necessarily translate into the wholesale replacement of jobs or the disappearance of entire industries, he says.

The same distinction applies to cybersecurity, Hamiel says. Although AI can help identify vulnerabilities, generate code and support security investigations, those capabilities do not mean that the complex problems facing security teams have suddenly become easy to solve.

In fact, some recent incidents described as "rogue" AI activity — such as OpenAI models autonomously hacking the Hugging Face framework, among others — may reveal a more familiar and persistent cybersecurity problem: organizations failing to address basic security weaknesses.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

"If you read some of the incident reports, these are organizations that weren't exercising basic security hygiene," Hamiel says.

In these cases, he argues, the weaknesses were already there, waiting to be discovered. "This wasn't just low-hanging fruit; this was fruit lying on the ground where anybody who looked for it would have found it," he says.

Rather than signaling an impending cybersecurity apocalypse, such incidents could prompt what Hamiel calls a "cybersecurity correction."

"It's not that there is this huge apocalypse happening; it's that many people weren't doing the right thing for a very long time," he explains.

In other words, AI may make it easier to discover and exploit existing weaknesses, exposing the consequences of inadequate security practices. The challenge for organizations is not simply to adopt new tools but to address the underlying problems those tools bring to light.

Indeed, the potential erosion of technical skills is not a problem that began with generative AI. Hamiel sees it as part of a longer trend in which technology increasingly mediates the relationship between professionals and the problems they are responsible for solving.

Hamiel's concern reflects what is often called the irony of automation: As systems take on more responsibility, the humans overseeing them can lose opportunities to practice the skills needed when those systems fail.

The consequences could extend beyond the skills of today's practitioners to the way the cybersecurity industry develops future experts, he says, especially in how lower-level work that AI can eliminate helps helping junior professionals learn.

Tasks that might appear repetitive or straightforward can provide essential experience, allowing new practitioners to understand how systems work before progressing to more complex investigations. "If you automate that, there isn't room for them to learn," Hamiel warns.

This creates a potential long-term problem for employers. AI may allow teams to complete certain tasks more efficiently today, but organizations still need experienced professionals who can investigate unfamiliar problems, evaluate automated findings, and respond when systems behave unexpectedly.

For cybersecurity pros to use generative AI effectively, then, it's simply a matter of applying it to tasks where it offers meaningful benefits while remaining aware of the skills that might be weakened if pros rely too much on these tools to do their jobs effectively.

"The goal here is to maximize the benefits and minimize the drawbacks," Hamiel says, something that is true for the use of any technology. "That's the framing that should be placed around this," he says.

Thus, the only way that organizations can adopt AI without losing essential cybersecurity expertise is to "apply them to the right types of activities," he says.

For cybersecurity pros, this means using generative AI for tasks such as threat hunting and threat intelligence, where preliminary analysis can help professionals work through information more efficiently, Hamiel notes. AI-powered penetration-testing tools are another area of promising development, extending beyond traditional vulnerability scanning to perform more complex tasks, he says.

Ultimately, the question is not whether AI will change cybersecurity, Hamiel says. That genie is most certainly already out of that bottle. Ultimately, the real challenge is ensuring that the industry does not become so dependent on increasingly capable tools that it loses the human expertise required to use them effectively, he says.

"Skills and expertise make your AI use more effective," Hamiel concludes. "If you have two professionals, and both use AI, the one with more knowledge of the task is going to make better use of the AI."

#9857. [$] Portable Python scripts with dependencies

A basic Python script is portable: it can be copied between machines with little concern about compatibility. A script that depends on third-party packages requires quite a bit more care and consideration, however. In 2023, PEP 723 ("Inline script metadata") introduced a standard for declaring a Python script's dependencies inside the script itself. Several third-party tools can now automatically install and manage those dependencies, but there is still little official support for this standard within Python itself.

#9856. Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

The dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

An alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

This reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

There is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below shows.

To make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

We applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

The two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

The 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

The practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

The accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

The takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

Want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

Hi there! From how I'm reading this, I think you might have missed a method error in your experiment that invalidates your headline.

The headline comparison looks like it has no control. The bf16 60B got one round of distillation and the MXFP4 60B got that round plus a second round from a better teacher. The obvious missing comparison is to give the bf16 60B the identical second distillation pass in bf16, same data, same steps, same teacher. Without that comparison you cannot separate "QAH is a good recipe" from "we trained one checkpoint longer against a teacher than the other."

Results table labels the teacher "120B teacher (MXFP4)", which is right since gpt-oss-120b ships with MXFP4 MoE weights natively. But the approach section says the teacher is full-size and full-precision, and the title claims the student beats its full-precision original. Those contradict.

Unless I'm wrong, I'd retract this and consdier republishing when you can show the significant difference on the comparable arms without extending one further than the other with more compute.

You're right that the headline table compares checkpoints with unequal training. The 60B bf16 checkpoint got one distillation pass (the recovery); the 60B MXFP4 checkpoint got that pass plus a second one against the 120B teacher. We describe that second pass in the approach section, but we should have been explicit that the table therefore doesn't, on its own, separate "distilling under quantization" from "distilling for longer." We'll add that caveat to the text.

A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The question we set out to answer is the one a deployment team faces: Given a compressed model that has to ship in 4 bits, what's the best way to run the quantization step? The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. What we shouldn't have leaned into is the stronger causal reading, that quantization itself is "free training", and you're right that the current table doesn't isolate that.

The comparison that would settle it is the one you describe: the bf16 60B given the identical second pass. same data, steps, teacher and, separately, that continued bf16 checkpoint post-training-quantized to MXFP4. The second is really the decision anyone deploying faces: heal under quantization, or quantize afterwards. If we extend this for a revised version, those are the arms we'd add; either way we're flagging them as a limitation of the current version rather than claiming the table resolves the question.

We don't think retraction is the right call. The reported numbers are real and reproducible, and the practical result stands. But we agree the causal framing needs that control, and we'd rather correct it in the open than argue it. Appreciate the push.

#9855. SBOMs Alone Can't Reveal the Scope of a Supply Chain Attack

A recent Shai-Hulud attack shows defenders need real-time visibility into production code and affected services to respond to supply chain compromises.

ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 — Denver — Depending on a software bill of materials (SBOM) to determine what happens when a malicious package slips past security checks can leave defenders struggling to establish what code actually executed, which systems it touched, and how far the compromise spread.

In a session at the ISC2 Security Congress 2026 this week, Atlassian product security manager Deepam Kanjani used a real-world compromise involving the Shai-Hulud worm to highlight incident response challenges, including gaps in runtime visibility, transitive dependency ownership, and attacker attribution.

In the session, Kanjani said he had altered all identifying details, figures, and the sequence of events to protect confidentiality, though his first-person, war-room narrative of underlying attack techniques, technical behaviors, and challenges was based on real events at a large-scale software-as-a-service (SaaS) environment.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Kanjani described the incident as involving a package that appeared legitimate, with a matching SHA hash, more than 3,400 GitHub stars, and a repository that looked credible to the company's security tooling. But hidden three layers deep in the package was a malicious transitive dependency named shai-hulud, after the giant sandworms in the Dune movie series. Because it was not a direct dependency, it did not surface in a top-level dependency audit.

The first inkling that something was wrong came when a behavioral scanner flagged the package as running something it shouldn't have been running. Incident responders initially dismissed the alert as a likely false positive because the hash matched and there was no other obvious indication of the package being malicious.

Additionally, the SBOM reported the environment as clean when the security team consulted it. What they did not realize at the time was that the SBOM was two development sprints out of date, Kanjani said.

As the response unfolded, the team could not say with confidence which services used the package. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) provided initial clues but could not establish which services were affected or how far the compromise had spread. Responders needed runtime evidence to determine what code had actually executed and what it could access.

Without that runtime telemetry, they had to correlate logs manually across more than 400 services, leaving them without a reliable picture of the compromise's potential reach. An initial Slack message from the incident response handler to enterprise stakeholders made matters worse by being too vague and prompting a set of parallel investigations into the still-unfolding event.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

The security team's efforts to identify the attacker by tracing registry ownership, npm maintainer history, publisher identities, and GitHub records quickly led them to dead ends. The repository had been copied from a legitimate project, and the publisher's identity and account history appeared to have been fabricated, Kanjani said.

Researchers have subsequently attributed at least some of the later Shai-Hulud attacks to a threat actor tracked as TeamPCP.

The key takeaway, according to Kanjani, is that organizations need to look beyond SBOMs and dependency inventories and instead base incident response around what actually runs in production. The focus should be to equip security teams to identify, scope, prioritize, and contain incidents and enable real-time visibility into affected services and the potential scope of a compromise.

"You are triaging a runtime graph. Not a dependency file. Your tools must reflect that," he said.

Kanjani recommended that organizations keep deployed SBOMs under 72 hours old and try to ensure that more than 98% of production services meet that threshold. He also recommended enabling runtime capabilities to detect unknown module loads in under 90 seconds and daily registry checks to detect lookalikes of internal package names within 24 hours of publication.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

Kanjani described these as targets that organizations should calibrate for their own environments rather than as universal benchmarks. In addition, security teams should focus on the operation rather than the operator, Kanjani said. "Identity signals rotate. Operational necessities don't. Build detection around what the worm must do to function — not who's driving it."

All communications with stakeholders regarding a security incident also need to be direct and unambiguous. The key is to be honest, he said, while making sure to present the details in language appropriate for the intended audience.

"Don't bullsh-t. Tell them the reality in a way they can absorb it," he said. "You don't want to sell panic."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

InfoQ Homepage News Vitest 5: Prioritises Performance with a Shared Vite Server, Trace View, and Stricter Test Defaults

Nov 03, 2026 2 min read

Vitest, the Vite-native testing framework maintained by VoidZero, has released Vitest 5.0, a major version that puts raw speed ahead of new surface area while quietly tightening several long-standing defaults.

Using a purpose-built benchmark suite that spans everything from a five-file utility package to a 1,280-module monolith, the team reports gains of roughly 8 to 25 percent across most setups, rising to 53 percent in VM pool scenarios. VoidZero summarised the release on X as "vm pools up to 53% faster, ~18% boost across the board including Browser Mode". The wins come from inline projects sharing a single Vite server, a stabilised on-disk fsModuleCache, fewer round trips between the main process and workers, and VM pools that reuse compiled code. A new vitest doctor command reruns a suite under alternative configurations and recommends faster options.

Browser Mode also gains a built-in Trace View that records each interaction and assertion as a DOM snapshot for step-by-step replay, while the new vi.when API lets a single spy return different values per argument.

clearMocks now defaults to true, unawaited async assertions fail rather than warn, hoisted vi.mock calls placed outside the top level now throw, and toThrow('') matches any error. As the independent OpenReplay breakdown puts it, most of these changes simply "break test code that was already wrong", but the dangerous ones are suites that pass locally on Vitest 4 and "go red in CI with an error that says nothing about why", usually call-count assertions that relied on mock history leaking between tests.

Vitest 5 requires Vite 6.4 and Node.js 22.12 or newer, and Yarn users must now install vite themselves because it became a peer dependency. The migration guide and v5.0.0 changelog document each change, and reporter output, attachments, and blob reports now live under one .vitest/ directory, so CI artifact paths need updating. Ecosystem catch-up is ongoing: Cloudflare's vitest-pool-workers issue notes its peer range pinned to v4 means any project pulling the new release "fails before a single test runs".

Against Jest, a recent head-to-head comparison scores Vitest ahead on performance and future-proofing yet behind on ecosystem and community, reflecting Jest's far larger install base and first-class React Native support. The advice to anyone considering the choice is unchanged, reach for Vitest on Vite, Nuxt, or greenfield projects, leave large working Jest suites in place, and let the two coexist in a monorepo.

Vitest is an open-source, Vite-powered test runner developed by VoidZero, the company founded by Vite creator Evan You that has joined Cloudflare. It reuses a project's existing Vite configuration to run unit, component, and browser tests with native ESM and TypeScript support, and is backed by more than 790 contributors.

#9852. External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Mail bombing is getting a new look with a wide-scale, ongoing social engineering campaign that might be tied to the Black Basta ransomware gang.

Threat actors are abusing Microsoft Teams' external chat functionality at scale, using IT-support impersonation and email bombing tactics to trick employees into granting remote access. Attackers target multiple users within short, five-minute windows of time, and once the victim bites, the attack chain reaches payload execution in under 15 minutes.

In a blog post on Oct. 26, Arctic Wolf detailed the campaign and what it described as a "recurring social engineering pattern" across more than 400 incidents in the wild. Threat actors use Microsoft Teams' external chat creation capability, which enables outside parties to contact employees.

"A consistent pattern of attacker behavior has emerged across these incidents: the use of the same throwaway tenants, the same 'IT Support (Internal)' display names, the same remote-access tools, and increasingly, the same payload domains," Arctic Wolf's Shubham Dubey wrote in the blog post.

Related:LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

In a typical example of the attack, the victim is "mail bombed," or inundated with a flood of email subscriptions or newsletters, to establish a sense of urgency. Then, an external Teams user claiming to be IT support contacts the victim and offers to address the issue. The impersonator persuades the employee to launch a remote-access session via legitimate tooling like Quick Assist (most common), AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport, and LogMeIn.

Once the victim grants access, the attacker conducts follow-on activity such as executing malware, stealing credentials, performing reconnaissance, or possibly deploying ransomware. Dubey explained that a typical order for this is a whoami/systeminfo-based recon, a PowerShell-based payload, a command-and-control (2) beacon, lateral movement to gain access to credentials through Kerberos abuse methods like Kerberoasting and GoldenPAC, and a second, commercial-grade remote access tool, "which provides an independent control channel that survives remediation of the original implant."

Spam or mail bombing is not a new tactic. Threat actors have been flooding inboxes as a pretense for social engineering for some time now. Microsoft researchers identified the use of this technique by Black Basta in mid-2024, with later examples seen in 3AM, Cactus, Chaos, and the GoGRPC campaigns. But what stands out about Arctic Wolf's research is that it shows this technique operating at scale, with recurring infrastructure, naming conventions, and attacker behavior seen across hundreds of incidents.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, tells Dark Reading roughly 15% of cases progressed beyond the initial stage into a successful compromise, which, given the volume of the campaign, constitutes a success.

As for who is behind recent attack waves, Moore could not make definitive attributions but says, "Black Basta-associated activity remains one of the most significant drivers of Teams chat abuse."

On the infrastructure front, Arctic Wolf noted a move from throwaway onmicrosoft.com tenants toward attacker-controlled domains, especially ".top" domains, and provided data on their prevalence. The vendor stated that approximately half of observed cases involving paid domains used .top domains.

For naming, attackers would reach out with "(Internal)" appended to the display name to trick the victim that a message is coming from within the company, even though Teams labels the sender as "external" simultaneously. The names will also frequently use friendly sounding names (Arctic Wolf offered Liam, Scott McGhee, and Matthew as examples) after labels like "IT Support" and "IT Service Desk."

Other markers observed included naming conventions specific to the target's locale ("Supporte TI" for French- and Spanish-speaking organizations), and the use of 100 different emojis in attacker display names.

Related:Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

Arctic Wolf noted that prior to engaging with victims, the attackers initiate a one-on-one chat to avoid group conversations, which Microsoft records in its telemetry as the ChatCreated event. Arctic Wolf assesses this to be the primary detection point for defenders setting alerts.

The vendor also recommended setting an allowlist for trusted external organizations, blocking chats with unmanaged or Teams consumer accounts, disabling the option that lets unmanaged users start conversations with your users, blocking federation with trial-only tenants, and hardening your remote access path.

In a nod to Cybersecurity Awareness Month, Arctic Wolf pointed out that it may also be wise to alert staff to the social engineering aspects behind these campaigns, including outlining exactly how IT reaches out, what these contacts look like (and what they do not look like), and to train users how to read the external sender tag in Teams to identify possible red flags. Microsoft Teams also includes end-user reporting in the application itself.

That said, the technique could yet progress further.

"We have also recently observed campaigns combining Teams chat abuse with ClickFix-style social engineering, suggesting that the technique continues to evolve and is being integrated with other intrusion methods," Moore says.

A Microsoft spokesperson tells Dark Reading that the company helps organizations reduce the risk of phishing and social engineering in Teams through layered, built-in protections that, for example, can let administrators block external Teams users. The spokesperson adds that, next month, "Teams is introducing AI-powered phishing detection that uses conversation context to identify phishing and social engineering in higher-risk messaging scenarios, particularly first-contact chats with external users."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston.
