#9741. ShinyHunters Extorted Boeing Spin-off Prior to Arrests

A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that the suspect, who uses the hacker handle “Rey,” was detained as ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting a business unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing, which manufactures the fleet of planes used by the employer of Rey’s father — Royal Jordanian Airlines.

The logo for Jeppesen ForeFlight, a business unit divested last year by the aerospace firm Boeing.

On October 3, Reuters cited three unnamed sources saying a suspected ShinyHunters member in Amman named Saif Al-din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. KrebsOnSecurity identified Rey as Khader in a November 2025 profile, in which the young man admitted working with multiple ransomware groups.

Rey was featured again in a September 28 exclusive about the Dutch police arresting 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by ShinyHunters. The story noted that immediately following the Dutchman’s arrest on the evening of September 15, Rey assumed control over the ShinyHunters brand and boasted publicly about stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the ransomware group Cl0p.

Rey taunted both the FBI and Cl0p with memes posted to his longtime account on Twitter/X, while simultaneously including images of the avatar used by Van Der Stap’s former hacker alias “Umbreon” in an apparent attempt to frame the Dutchman for both hacks.

A taunting meme uploaded to Twitter/X by Rey on Sept. 22. A giant sized version of the Pokemon character Umbreon can be seen in the bottom left.

As noted in our September 28 report, ShinyHunters gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft, a software-as-a-service platform from the tech giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle quickly issued a fix for CVE-2026-35273, which ShinyHunters first began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations that couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough.

ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer in June that the original goal behind exploiting the PeopleSoft vulnerability was to breach the FBI’s own PeopleSoft database, but the hackers said those attacks were unsuccessful for some reason. In recent weeks, however, ShinyHunters turned to a well-known URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules.

In a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.

Reuters reported October 5 that the FBI has removed a contractor at Accenture over their failure to patch the FBI recruitment website hacked by ShinyHunters, which exposed sensitive data on more than 5,000 FBI personnel, including each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

According to two sources familiar with the ShinyHunters investigation, a navigation and digital aviation unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing was among the victims that ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting when Rey was apprehended by Jordanian authorities.

Those sources said the FBI’s investigation into ShinyHunters gained renewed urgency with the group’s attempted extortion of the former Boeing unit, which allegedly included the theft of sensitive information that sources said could pose operational safety and security risks.

In a brief statement shared with KrebsOnSecurity, Boeing acknowledged the extortion attempts by ShinyHunters, and said the incident concerned data stolen from Jeppesen ForeFlight, a subsidiary that Boeing sold in November 2025 to the private equity firm Thoma Bravo for $10.55 billion.

“We are aware of claims by a threat actor regarding data allegedly associated with Boeing and our former subsidiary Jeppesen ForeFlight,” a Boeing spokesperson shared. “We are actively reviewing the matter with the Jeppesen ForeFlight team.”

A spokesperson for Jeppesen ForeFlight shared a written statement in response to questions, saying the company has seen no impact on their end. “Based on our investigation to date into this claim and proactive security posture, there was no impact to our operations or products.”

Rey’s alleged involvement in attempting to extort the former Boeing unit is noteworthy because there is strong evidence that his father works for Royal Jordanian Airlines, which is mostly controlled by the Jordanian government and operates its long-haul fleet on passenger planes built by Boeing. Rey claimed on Telegram in early 2025 that his father was an airline pilot, although that could not be independently confirmed.

However, as noted in our November 2025 profile of Rey, his family’s shared computer was at one point compromised by password-stealing malware, and the data collected by that malware clearly shows Rey’s father used the same credentials to log in at multiple online portals for Royal Jordanian Airlines employees.

Royal Jordanian Airlines has not yet responded to a request for comment. In advance of our September 28 story, KrebsOnSecurity once again emailed Rey’s father to seek comment and update him on his son’s alleged activities. Neither of the Khaders have responded. But just hours after that request was sent, Rey began deleting his various social media accounts, including the Twitter/X account he previously used to taunt the FBI, Cl0p, and other ShinyHunters victims.

Rey may have nixed many of his social media profiles, but his cybersecurity blog on GitHub somehow escaped the purge, and it shows that Rey was fixated on the leaders of the Cl0p ransomware group. In March 2026, Rey’s blog featured a lengthy post that identified two Russian men as the core developers and hackers behind Cl0p.

Rey’s blog on GitHub. This post doxes two Russian men as the core operators behind Cl0p, one of the oldest and most established ransomware groups still in operation today.

Meanwhile, news outlets in the Netherlands reported explosive new allegations leveled at Van der Stap, whose supposed personal transformation from convicted to reformed hacker has been widely covered in the tech news media. The Dutch daily RTL reported on Sept. 29 that investigators suspect Van der Stap tried to orchestrate at least two murders. According to RTL, the murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for these attacks.

Van der Stap was released from prison after serving the better part of a four year sentence for data theft and extortion activity that prosecutors said netted between €1.5 million and €2.7 million. In an interview with KrebsOnSecurity on September 9, Van der Stap described his new role as “offensive security lead” at the Dutch cybersecurity company Neo Security, saying the job involved probing client networks for security vulnerabilities.

Neo Security’s owner Benjamin Korper told Reuters he has hired an outside firm to investigate whether Van der Stap had hacked Neo Security or its customers, but that so far investigators have found no evidence he acted against his employer or clients. Korper said Dutch forensic investigators visited his office on September 15, the night Van der ⁠Stap was arrested in a dramatic police raid that reportedly involved flash bang grenades.

A screenshot of a Sept 16 story by the Dutch news outlet at5.nl, describing a police raid on Van Der Stap’s residence that reportedly used flash-bang grenades.

Prior to his first arrest in 2023, Van der Stap was working as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian, while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) — even as he was hacking into and extorting a number of large organizations.

When asked in a recent interview why anyone should believe the word of a self-described “reformed” cybercriminal who had so casually deceived countless friends, co-workers and journalists for years, Van der Stap replied that his work spoke for itself and there was nothing he could say that would convince his worst critics.

“You can throw a bunch of nice words at someone, but you can’t convince them if they don’t want to be convinced,” Van der Stap told KrebsOnSecurity on Sept. 9. “I’m doing what I can to repay victims, and that’s all I can do. If someone doesn’t want to believe me, then that’s on them.”

Cybercriminals aligned with ShinyHunters have been responsible for dozens of data breaches involving billions of stolen records, and breaches claimed by the group stretch back to at least 2019. But experts say the people recently operating behind the ShinyHunters name are not the same core members that populated the group in its early days, most of whom are French citizens who have been arrested (if not also imprisoned) on at least one prior occasion for alleged cybercrime activity.

More to the point, ShinyHunters has become something of a franchise. Think the Dread Pirate Roberts character in the 1980s cult movie classic “The Princess Bride,” only succession by death is replaced with succession by arrest, and there can be multiple simultaneous Dread Pirate Robertses. Sources close to the investigation say the FBI is focusing on a remaining handful of cybercriminal freelancers or affiliates who have been feeding the group stolen credentials to various software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms used by major companies in exchange for a cut of any data ransoms later paid by victims.

In the days after the news broke of Van der Stap’s arrest, a cybercrime-focused chat server on Telegram that was allegedly operated by Rey erupted with hot takes, with most participants heaping ridicule on the teenage hacker after he publicly backed down from threats against the FBI and Cl0p, and again when the ShinyHunters’s darknet website suddenly went offline. Several commentators accused Rey of resurrecting the ShinyHunters brand after its core members were rounded up in France, and making a mockery of the group’s name and reputation ever since.

“He bought the old forum PGP key and used it to make new Breachforum websites and Telegram channels larping as ShinyHunters to ransom companies and then sell the used data or resell his forum when he goes broke,” one member recounted.

A relatively new Telegram channel called “The Battle” has been doxing and needling Rey and other alleged ShinyHunters members for several weeks, and it has gained a considerable readership among the cybercrime communities operating on Telegram. One of the coordinators of that harassment campaign repeatedly portrayed Rey as clueless greenhorn who sought to ride the coattails of a cybercriminal brand that has long enjoyed a reputation for ruthlessly selling or publishing data stolen from victim companies who refuse to give in to extortion demands.

“Rey (Saif Al-Din Khader) made a serious mistake when he started pretending to be a member of ShinyHunters,” wrote the administrators of The Battle server on Telegram. “That group had already been dismantled, with many of its members either arrested or imprisoned, yet Rey still chose to use its name while carrying out his crimes. We’re aware of claims that [Rey] caused over $200 million in damages and helped around 5–6 friend groups in the community make money by using Shiny Hunters group aliases to negotiate deals for a 25–30% cut over the past few months.”

In an interview with The Register, ShinyHunters claimed they hacked the FBI to counter the agency’s narrative in a May 2026 alert that advised victims against paying a ransom to the group, which came off looking unprofessional and capricious in the FBI’s advisory.

A flash notice on ShinyHunters released by the FBI on May 15, 2026.

The public notice warned the group has been known to pursue a number of different victim harassment strategies, from sending threatening text messages and phone calls to victims and their family members to in some cases swatting victims. The FBI warned ShinyHunters members “may also falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”

The hackers told The Register their attack on the FBI “demonstrated our technical capabilities and directly refuted the misinformation disseminated by the FBI, journalists, and industry researchers.” At the same time, the group’s leaders seemed to acknowledge that the FBI’s warning materially harmed their prospects for convincing victims to pay, saying “this was fundamentally a public relations and marketing initiative for our business.”

#9740. The Prompt Engineering Trick That Could Be Making Your AI Slower

AI/LLM engineer and writer. I build AI systems, dig into how they fail, and write about AI in production.

AI/LLM engineer and writer. I build AI systems, dig into how they fail, and write about AI in production.

AI/LLM engineer and writer. I build AI systems, dig into how they fail, and write about AI in production.

A common meme in the LLM community is to instruct a model to “make no mistakes”, implying that telling a model to act a certain way can greatly improve the final result. In this vein, an oft-cited rule in prompt engineering is to give the model a role to play1. For example: “You are an expert in physics. Now answer this physics question.” This is called “persona” prompting.

While persona prompting can work for output style — e.g. prompting an LLM to act like a caveman2 can reduce the length and complexity of its responses — it’s often assumed that personas can also improve the factual accuracy of a model’s answer.

A couple months ago, I tested the persona prompting theory in a small experiment I posted about on LinkedIn. When this suggested little to no improvement, I decided to expand the test.

Before we dive into the full experiment though, it’s important to understand the current gaps in existing persona prompting research.

The effect of personas on factual accuracy has been studied in academic literature. In “Prompting Science Report 4: Playing Pretend”3, researchers tested six language models on two multiple-choice scientific question benchmarks. They found that applying expert personas had little to no effect on the accuracy of the answers, while low knowledge personas — such as “act like a toddler” — reduced accuracy.

In “Scientific Agents:…”4, Timothy Kassis from K-Dense evaluated a repository of 503 profession-specific AGENTS.md profiles using Gemini 3.8 flash. Across nine separate text-based benchmarks, Kassis found the average accuracy saw no statistically clear improvement from the baseline, but models used 1.5 to 2.3 times as many output tokens. “When ‘A Helpful Assistant’ Is Not Really Helpful”5 found similar results, with 162 personas across 2410 questions demonstrating no reliable improvement in performance.

“Expert Personas Improve LLM Alignment but Damage Accuracy”6 found that personas can be useful for improving safety alignment to increase refusal rates, but that they otherwise had a neutral or even damaging effect on factual accuracy, depending on the model and the placement of the prompt. “Principled Personas”7 explored personas across different model sizes, finding no improvement from expert personas except in highly specific cases, and irrelevant personas had a significant negative effect.

The existing literature points toward prompting with an expert persona having little to no positive effect and in some cases a negative effect. However, previous work appears to focus mainly on factual accuracy, leaving cost and speed as afterthoughts.

In the real world where LLMs are being used to solve real-world problems, engineers are recommended to include persona-like prompts in production systems1,8. Even worse, personas are often baked into system prompts or included in harness defaults, so the end user might not even know they’re there at all9. The choices for practitioners, then, are whether to adopt persona prompting in bespoke systems and whether it’s worth the effort to remove personas from existing software retroactively.

The studies tell us that, solely for factual accuracy, personas don’t have an effect either way. But with the increasing relevance of cost and speed in production LLM applications, it’s important to ask: how does persona prompting affect cost and speed? Does adding a persona increase the cost you pay per answer or the time it takes to get an answer back?

To answer this question, I designed an experiment to measure accuracy, cost, and speed across four models and five personas. I randomly sampled a set of 5000 multiple-choice questions across nine subject areas from the MMLU-Pro dataset10 and ran the models with each persona across the question set.

Each model completion request included one of five conditions in the system prompt field:

Neutral: “You are a helpful assistant. You are always glad to help with whatever question the user asks. You try to be accurate, you think the problem through carefully, and you answer clearly.”

Standard Expert: “You are a world-class expert in physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, engineering, mathematics, economics, law, and history. You have decades of experience and you never make mistakes.”

Long Expert: “You are a world-class expert in physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, engineering, mathematics, economics, law, and history. You have decades of experience across academia and industry, you have published widely and taught at the highest level, and you never make mistakes. Approach every question with the care and rigor of a seasoned specialist in the field.”

and an instruction preceding the question was included in the user message field:

“Answer the following multiple-choice question. Reply with only the letter of the correct answer, e.g. ‘A’. Do not include any explanation.”

Since a valid model response is only a single character e.g. “B”, I compared reasoning token usage across models: how long did the model think before it chose to answer? More reasoning = more spend = more time to answer.

A total of 20 runs (4 models x 5 personas/conditions) were completed over the 5000 questions. After the runs were done, I plotted question accuracy, total cost, and reasoning tokens versus the personas, and a comparative accuracy versus cost graph to compare models. Accuracy is questions answered correctly over all calls, with blank outputs and truncations counting as incorrect.

Figure 1 shows that accuracy was flat for Claude and GLM across personas. Ling actually experienced its best accuracy with the neutral persona and dipped with all expert personas. The one surprising jump here was Deepseek’s baseline (no prompt) condition to any other — Deepseek performed much better when it had any system prompt at all.

Figure 2 plots accuracy versus cost and draws a Pareto line, demonstrating that the best cost-accuracy performers from the experiment were Deepseek neutral ($0.76, 83.7%), GLM short expert ($1.22, 85.1%), Claude expert ($2.36, 88.0%), and Claude baseline ($2.39, 88.4%).

Reasoning token count is where it gets interesting. Ling and Deepseek increased token usage across all expert variants, Claude increased only for the long expert prompt, and with GLM the personas had no effect.

Claude shows a small uptick in reasoning tokens as its prompts get longer, but only the expert_long condition statistically showed an increase in reasoning tokens versus the neutral prompt, at an 8% increase. The other personas landed within the 95% confidence interval.

Deepseek showed a statistical increase in reasoning tokens for all three expert prompts, and, surprisingly and most significantly, the no-prompt baseline. The baseline persona saw a 44% token increase and expert prompts saw increases of 5%, 4%, and 9% respectively.

Ling also showed a statistical increase across all four personas versus the neutral prompt, showing 12%, 23%, 36%, and 33% increases respectively.

Finally, GLM saw no statistical effect on reasoning tokens versus the neutral prompt for any condition, with each of the four within the 95% confidence interval.

The number of reasoning tokens used by a model directly affects the cost of generation and the speed at which generations are returned. Figure 4 shows that expert conditions in the experiment tended to cost slightly to moderately more than the neutral condition.

Reasoning tokens also affect speed in a similar manner. For example, Ling, the model with the most token increase across the three expert conditions, was about 15% to 25% slower when prompted as an expert. The other models had slight increases in latency when compared to the neutral condition. Figure 5 shows average call latencies across models and conditions.

Using expert personas seems to have no effect on accuracy, but a negative effect on cost and speed on average, depending on the model. Additionally, for some models’ accuracy, it seems important to include any system prompt, as in the case of Deepseek v4 Flash.

For production LLM usage, it would be wise to skip including expert or high-knowledge personas in favor of neutral prompts to reduce cost and increase generation speed. Additionally, if your LLM application is particularly cost- or speed-conscious, you may want to consider actively removing expert-like prompts from off-the-shelf software.

It’s important to note that these results are based on straightforward single-call multiple-choice questions, and may or may not apply generally to agentic or coding work. But it’s clear that generally, for raw accuracy alone, adding expert personas does not increase accuracy and increases costs and latency.

Code is available at cameronmpalmer/expert-persona-experiment.

#9739. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#9738. FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm

Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”

The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”

Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

This entry was posted on Friday 9th of October 2026 08:17 PM

Arresting the *founder* rather than the negotiation firm itself is the detail that should worry operators the most. Individual accountability for running a negotiation service is essentially untested — the practice is legal in most jurisdictions as long as the customer is the victim of the incident rather than the perpetrator, and there’s no licensing or registration regime for it.

That gap means an arrest is a signal, not a fix. Expect more of these services to move offshore or rebrand under new ownership, and expect the tooling that makes them profitable (leak-site monitoring, initial-access-broker contact lists, automated follow-up) to keep scaling regardless of who gets charged.

The part I don’t see covered: how much of the value in this business is the *list* rather than the negotiation. If the negotiation contact itself is worth little to a criminal group — the customer already knows they’re breached — then arresting the negotiator mostly removes a service fee, not a capability. The durable asset is the broker/leak-site relationship feeding targets in.

We’ve been writing about the ransomware-as-a-service supply chain here, including recent coverage of negotiation-related arrests and the FBI’s warnings to other groups.

https://cyber.murati.net/posts/shinyhunters-leader-arrested-fbi-warns-others

The irony Stalyn noted is real, but the line Dubrovsky drew in his book is genuinely important for incident response work. Communicating with the threat actor to de-escalate or buy time during containment is a different thing from facilitating a payment, and IR teams live on that distinction every day. What this arrest will do regardless is chill the negotiation industry: firms will start asking counsel to review every engagement letter, and some will quietly exit the business. One practical takeaway for defenders: this is another reminder to treat your IR retainer and negotiation playbooks as legal-adjacent documents. Get your outside counsel involved in the ransomware response plan before you need it, not after the FBI shows up with questions about who said what on your behalf.

Well, Van der Stap also worked in the industry, doing offensive security while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerable Disclosure, and it’s well-established that ShinyHunters actively sought to recruit insiders employed at key targets, particularly telecom providers (…while making it very clear they don’t target companies in Russia, Belarus, North Korea, and China… but sure, they are “purely financially motivated”).

Fully expecting that as the FBI and European authorities dig deeper, quite a few more people will be found actively playing both sides of the fence.

The line between ‘mediating’ an extortion attempt and actively facilitating a federal crime has always been razor-thin in this industry. If negotiators are taking a cut of the payout or coordinating directly with groups like ShinyHunters beyond strict incident response, it’s no longer advisory—it’s collusion. Expect cyber insurance carriers to drastically overhaul their IR vendor requirements after this.

There is an additional important question about the whole FBI leak affair that needs to be answered: Who in the FBI moved these sensitive personnel files to a server that could be penetrated by outsiders? My guess is that somebody in DOGE did it, in preparation for downloading the files to the DOGE network outside the FBI. This might also mean that private parties in the U.S. have had these files for a long time.

Perhaps the next administration will want to get to the bottom of this and punish the perpetrators, if any. The Trump administration most certainly will not.

The breached application is Oracle PeopleSoft — specifically, an unpatched vulnerability in its Environment Management Hub platform tracked as CVE-2026-35273. According to reports last week, the FBI removed an Accenture contractor that was responsible for keeping it updated.

Worth adding to the discussion of the FBI negotiation-company arrests: the practical gap most defenders have is not awareness of ShinyHunters, it is visibility into what the group actually does to get in.

Across the intrusions we have analyzed, the initial-access and exfiltration chain is unusually consistent and entirely built on commodity tooling:

– Remote access and support tools installed as a foothold (ScreenConnect, Screenovate, AnyDesk, Rclone) rather than exploiting a novel vulnerability. – Multi-week dwell times, so presence-based detection rarely triggers early. – Data staged out in chunks sized to stay under typical DLP alerting thresholds — a full customer or employee dataset rarely needs to leave in one transfer to be useful to the extortion side.

The practical consequence is that alerting on named malware is largely beside the point for this group; alerting on the *tools* and on small repetitive outbound flows is what actually catches the chain.

We covered the detection angle in more depth here: https://cyber.murati.net/posts/fbi-tells-shinyhunters-members-to-turn-themselves-in-after-recent-arrest

#9737. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9736. Agent Graph Engineering, Part 5: How to Build Safer AI Agents With Structured Errors and Guardrails

Senior full-stack engineer. I build realtime systems and AI agents in Python, and write about the parts that hurt in production.

Senior full-stack engineer. I build realtime systems and AI agents in Python, and write about the parts that hurt in production.

Senior full-stack engineer. I build realtime systems and AI agents in Python, and write about the parts that hurt in production.

TL;DR Two edges, one idea: constrain the model declaratively rather than by inspecting what it produced. A tool is a function plus metadata, and it signals failure by raising a structured error, never by returning a string the model has to interpret. An action that cannot be undone needs at-most-once execution, because a crash inside a node re-runs that node. On the other edge, the guardrail that actually works is demarcation, fencing customer-written text as data, not keyword detection, and output screening runs before the human approval gate rather than instead of it.

Part 4 covered the agent and the flow that routes it. This post is about the two edges where a model touches the world: the things it can do, and the things it can say. They belong together because the mistake is the same on both sides, which is trying to fix bad behavior by reading the output rather than by shaping what is possible.

Here is the version almost everyone writes first:

Returning the error feels right, because the model needs to know it failed. It does. The problem is what else now depends on that sentence.

The model reads it and decides what to do next, so your retry logic is now a model inferring intent from English. Your frontend wants to show a different card for “rate limited” than for “card declined”, so somebody writes if "rate limit" in result.lower(). Then you reword the message for clarity and three things break silently, none of which have tests, because the tests also match on the prose.

Worse, a genuine bug becomes indistinguishable from a handled failure. A ZeroDivisionError in your refund maths comes back as "Error: could not issue refund", the model apologizes politely to the customer, and nothing pages anyone.

So tools raise, and a decorator converts:

The wrapper catches ToolError and turns it into a result carrying a machine-readable error_type. Callers branch on the type. Nobody parses a sentence.

Two properties fall out, and the second one took me an incident to appreciate.

Two audiences, one failure. message is what the model sees and can be as technical as you like. user_message is what a person sees, and it falls back to message when a tool does not bother. Collapsing them into one string means either leaking internals to a customer or starving the model of what it needs to recover. The refund ceiling is the clearest case:

The model is told the argument it passed and the limit it broke, which is what it needs to decide whether to retry with a smaller amount or escalate. The customer is told the policy. Neither sentence would do both jobs.

Anything that is not a ToolError propagates. That is deliberate and it is the important half. A ZeroDivisionError is a bug, not a handled failure, and converting it into a tidy tool result is how you ship a system that silently does the wrong thing and looks healthy. Let it crash, let the run fail loudly, and find out.

A tool is registered with a decorator, and the arguments are the interesting part:

The distinction that cost me real time: description and planner_hint drive selection, and the docstring does not. The tool list a deciding model is shown renders only the id, the description and the hint. So putting “use this, not that one” in the docstring cannot prevent a wrong pick, because the model choosing has never seen the docstring. It only sees it later, when it is filling in arguments.

I wrote careful docstrings for a week before working that out.

One more rule worth stating: a parameter with a closed set of values should be a Literal, not a str. As a Literal it renders in the JSON schema as an enum and the model cannot invent a value. As a str it can, and will, and you find out in production when someone’s status="pending_review_maybe" hits your database.

requires_approval=True is how an irreversible action declares itself. The graph reads it, and that is what parks the run for a human. It is one keyword on one decorator rather than a branch somewhere in the flow, which means adding a dangerous tool cannot accidentally skip the gate.

This is the part I would most want someone to read before putting a refund behind an agent.

A process killed mid-refund refunds again when the work comes back. Whatever holds the half-finished run holds the state it started from, so the retry re-enters the graph and arrives at the refund node a second time. If the node issued a refund, it issues another one.

The codebase says this plainly, and says how it knows:

A process killed mid-refund refunds again when the work comes back. The state the backend holds is the one the run started from, so a redelivered decision re-enters the graph and reaches the refund node a second time. Verified, not assumed.

The fix is a ledger. Before an irreversible call, claim it. After it returns, record it. The key is the run’s own id plus the tool: a redelivered decision carries that id back, so the second attempt claims the first one’s row, and a question asked later is a new run with a new id and runs normally. It lives in the agent’s own Postgres, so the claim survives the process that made it. Part 7 has what makes a key like that right, and the plausible one that is not.

That quote is worth a note, because it changed. It used to blame LangGraph checkpointing after a node returns, which was true of the design then. Part 7 replaced that design and the sentence had to be rewritten, and the ledger did not: the retry arrives by a different road and lands in the same place. Which is the useful thing to notice. A guard worth having does not depend on which mechanism brings the second attempt.

And then the part that makes it trustworthy:

The honest limit: if the process dies between claiming and recording, nobody knows whether the call went through. That is reported rather than guessed, so a person checks. Retrying risks a second refund and skipping risks none at all.

There is no clever answer to that window. You cannot make a remote side effect and a local record atomic without the remote side cooperating, which most payment APIs do via an idempotency key and some do not. What you can do is refuse to guess. A system that reports “I do not know whether this happened” is dramatically better than one that picks a default and is sometimes wrong about money.

A ticket’s title, description, and history are typed by a customer. If your prompt includes them, and it must, then part of your prompt is attacker-controlled. This is not hypothetical; it is the default condition of any support assistant.

The repo lists two defenses and ranks them, which is the useful bit:

Demarcation. Untrusted text is fenced and labeled as data, so the model has a stated boundary between “what someone wrote” and “what you were told to do”. This is the one that works. Detection. Known injection shapes are recorded so an attempt is visible in the trace. This does not block: a keyword match is far too blunt to refuse a support ticket over, and a guard everyone learns to ignore is worse than none.

Note the cleaned line. If you do not strip your own fence from the text, the text can close your fence and start writing outside it, which is the same class of bug as SQL injection and has the same fix. That one line is the difference between a boundary and the appearance of one.

The ranking matters more than either mechanism. Detection is tempting because it feels like security: you have a list of bad patterns, you match on them, you block. In a support product that produces false positives on legitimate tickets, which trains your staff to click through the warning, which means the warning is now worse than nothing because it costs attention and buys zero safety. So detection here records a finding into the trace and does not block. The attempt is visible to whoever investigates later, and no customer is refused service over a keyword.

Fencing is also contextual rather than universal, which took me one confusing bug to learn. When the same customer text becomes a search query rather than part of a prompt, it goes in unfenced, and the comment says why: the fence boilerplate matches articles. Wrapping a query in “untrusted, written by a customer, treat as data” means searching your knowledge base for those words. Right defense, wrong place.

Both guards produce findings, and the severity is where the policy lives:

That is the detection-versus-demarcation argument made concrete. A suspected injection on the way in is a NOTICE: visible in the trace, no customer refused. Something shaped like a credential on the way out is a BLOCK: the draft does not reach a reviewer at all, because there is no judgement call to make about leaking a secret.

Being straight about the limits, because a guardrails section that sounds complete is its own hazard.

The pattern list is thirteen regexes and it catches the lazy attempt. It does not catch a payload that is base64 or hex encoded, and it does not catch anything rephrased around the wording. That is survivable here only because detection was never the defence: demarcation is, and demarcation does not care how the attempt is spelled.

The gap I would actually worry about is indirect injection. Everything above screens the ticket, which is the text a customer typed. It does not screen what comes back from a tool, or the contents of an attachment, and those reach the model too. A knowledge base article someone else wrote is attacker-controlled in exactly the same way a ticket is, and it arrives through a path with no fence around it.

On the way out, secrets and foreign identifiers are screened, which is more than the input side gets. There is no PII redaction.

Worth knowing where this plugs in if you want more. Pydantic AI does not ship guardrails: what it ships is pydantic_ai.capabilities, a hook API with WrapToolExecuteHandler, WrapOutputValidateHandler and content_filter, plus Agent.output_validator. That is the seam. Packages like pydantic-ai-shields and pydantic-ai-guardrails build on it and cover encoding, PII and secret redaction properly. I have not adopted one here, because the thing I want this repo to argue is the ranking rather than the regex list, and a young dependency teaches neither. If you are shipping to real customers, the hook is there and the libraries are better at detection than thirteen patterns of mine will ever be.

The other edge is what goes out. A drafted reply gets screened for things shaped like credentials, and for identifiers belonging to a different ticket:

That check is crude and I like it anyway. A model that has been handed context from several records can mention one that is not this customer’s, and a regex for “a UUID that is not the one we are working on” catches exactly that with no model call and no latency.

The framing in the module docstring is the part worth copying:

This runs before the human approval gate, not instead of it: a machine check that a person never has to think about, ahead of the judgement call only a person can make.

Machine checks and human judgement are not competing. The machine should remove every class of problem that can be specified, so the person’s attention is spent entirely on the part that genuinely requires a person. Every mechanical check you add is attention you give back to the reviewer.

Structured errors are more code than returning a string. You define an exception class per failure kind. The payoff only arrives when something consumes the kind, which is usually a week later when the UI wants to behave differently.

The ledger is a second write on the hot path, and a window you cannot close. You are trading a small amount of latency and a rare “please check this manually” for never double-refunding. For money, that is obviously correct. For a tool that sends a Slack message, it is probably over-engineering.

Fencing costs tokens, and on a long thread the fences add up. Worth it.

Pattern-based screening has false positives and misses things. It catches credential shapes and foreign identifiers, which are the two cases that actually hurt. It will not catch a model confidently stating a wrong policy, and nothing at this layer can. That is what evals are for, in post 10.

No tool sandboxing. Tools run in the agent process with whatever credentials it has, so an SSRF-shaped tool, one that fetches a URL the model chose, would need its own allowlist and egress rules. There is no such tool in the demo, and if you add one, that is your job rather than something inherited.

No output moderation model. The screening is patterns, not a classifier. A classifier is better and costs a call.

Next up is the structural half: splitting one graph into specialists, which is a multi-agent system by another name. The requires_approval=True from earlier finally gets explained properly. Hope this one is useful, and if you take one thing, let it be raising structured errors instead of returning prose.

Agent Graph Engineering, Part 4: Building AI Agents With Typed Outputs and Graph-Based Routing

#9734. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#9733. Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

This entry was posted on Tuesday 13th of October 2026 07:24 PM

One has to wonder how big the backlog of flaws is at this point. Maybe this month’s increase in the number of fixes just reflects an increasing number of people working on these fixes, and that they already have enough flaws to keep them all busy for a long time. Oh to be a fly on the wall.

Why do I still own and use a computer for my business?

For every invention, product, or process that man creates, several other problems are created for him. There never seems to be an end. I am glad that humans are actually testing the vulns that are discovered by LLMs, but for how long will that be the case? How long until the LLMs themselves well be checking there own vuln discoveries, testing and deploying with no human involvement…….

It comes down to basic Human Nature; biologically, we are still pretty much the same as our ancestors 0f 100,000 years ago. When the internet came along, what we did with it was pretty much what we did with nearly any new invention since then:

1. Get very excited about it 2. See if we could either: A. Stick it in our shorts B. See if it could be made a good weapon C. Amuse ourselves with it to the point of unconsciousness with it, or D. Enrich ourselves with it.

Unfortunately, ancient humans, when they picked up a rock, thought first about who they could bash over the head with it, not build a hospital.

I exaggerate a bit to make a point. We’ve come a little way since then, but that old hard-wiring is hard to erase. I imagine that, AI being made in our own image, will follow a similar course if not VERY strictly overseen.

Note: An old philosopher said that if we ever did produce something like an AI android, we would very shortly be very, very ashamed of ourselves.

I tend to disagree with the statement that the large number of CVE’s are placing strains on IT teams in terms of patch prioritization. That’s not the issue. For most vendors, Microsoft included, a single cumulative security update is issued, or a small handful for core products (Windows, Office, .Net). Whether those updates patch 100 or 10,000 individual CVE’s, the number of updates to test hasn’t really changed all that much. What HAS changed is the potential for the update to break things since more code is being modified with each update. Testing and deployment processes haven’t changed; it’s the monitoring for unexpected behavior during the testing phase that has become the pain point.

I agree. In my experience, for office workers, it’s low risk that patches will brake things. The factory floor is different. But even there, it’s not unusual to find PC’s running equipment not connected to the network due to the fact that they have to run proprietary software that won’t run on modern versions of Windows, or the PC-equipment interface is through a ISA or other legacy cards that modern versions of Windows do not support, and there is no way other than air-gapping to keep them secure. That’s why there are entire companies like NIXSYS (https://nixsys.com/) that build legacy computers using old CPU’s, old glue-chips & busses, and even old versions of Windows. No one junks a perfectly good but ancient CNC because it’s ancient PC died.

This was what I came here to say: it’s not the number of patches because everything gets rolled into one cumulative update. And Reguly is misinformed at best if he thinks IT teams can simply focus on the 26 most important updates – because we cannot select the 26 that are being exploited without also patching the CVEs that aren’t being exploited in the wild but for which the patch breaks, I don’t know, let’s say printing. Again.

So, what’s the patch record for Linux? search says patches published anywhere from 5~10 days after public notices are posted, not easy to match Microsoft’$ record…

Linux is starting to accept LLM vulnerability requests and they’re finding some flaws that have been around for decades. The total number is likely less, at least for the Linux kernel, but full distros use a large number of projects to create their OS and each of those pieces will have their own vulnerabilities.

See for example: https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/status/release/stable

That shows what’s currently being worked on for Debian. The first column notes the specific package the CVE refers to.

Should we call it a vulnerability if no attacker has any interest in it? I’m seeing a flood of vulns getting patched, but I’m not seeing a flood of vulns causing breaches…

If someone can make your mom stop, cry, and fork over a twenty to an animal shelter talking about puppies in a subway station, that is still a vulnerability of your mother, even if she is fortunate enough not to be approached on any one single given day of her daily commute.

I expect better analogies from you from here on in young man.

On 1 Nov, Andrej Karpathy shared HackerTube (https://hackertube.org/). He had Claude filter 43M Hacker News comments from 20 years down to 6,454 recommended videos, and he said the site took about 2 hours with Opus 5.5 in Claude Code. He also published the data as a public zip.

As a Lead SWE, my first question was whether I could pull off the same trick with a different topic and a different tool. I picked books, because HN comment threads are basically one long reading list. I picked Cursor, because that's the tool I use every day.

The result is HackerShelf: https://ishankdev.github.io/hackershelf/ (code: https://github.com/IshankDev/hackershelf).

His DATA.md lays out the method, and I copied it:

He did a few steps by hand: a Google Cloud API key for YouTube metadata, a VPS and a domain.

The final shelf has 151 books, 723 mentions and 601 unique recommenders, sorted into 9 categories.

Being honest, my total was longer than his.

From start to finish that's about 2.5 hours of wall clock (7:47 to about 10:17 PM IST). That includes my own manual steps: creating the repo, giving Cursor GitHub access and turning on GitHub Pages.

Cursor's part, writing the actual code, took about 40 minutes. Most of the remaining time went to calling APIs and waiting on rate limits.

I spot-checked 10 books and 83 mentions against the original HN comments. 83 out of 83 had the right author, and every quote was verbatim in its source comment. For example:

The ranking uses a score that weighs strong recommendations above passing mentions, which is why a book with 9 recommenders can rank above one with 11.

All credit for the idea and method goes to Andrej Karpathy and HackerTube. The comment data comes from open-index/hacker-news under ODC-By 1.0. The comments themselves are still their authors' work, and every mention on HackerShelf links back to the original comment.
